items.title: The Violent, Terrifying Acceleration Of Everything
items.content_text:
The Violent, Terrifying Acceleration Of Everything

Submitted by QTR's Fringe Finance

For decades, it has felt as though the world has been moving remarkably slowly.

Consider commercial aviation. Take someone from 1985, put them on a commercial flight today, and there is very little about the experience they wouldn’t recognize. The planes are more fuel-efficient, the avionics are more sophisticated and air traffic control has improved.

But other than the fact that men don’t wear three piece suits to travel and there’s no more ashtrays on your tray tables (yes, this was a thing) the fundamental experience is largely unchanged. In fact, we used to fly commercially across the Atlantic at twice the speed of sound. We don’t even do that anymore.

Now consider theoretical physics. The first half of the 20th century completely revolutionized our understanding of the universe. We developed general relativity, quantum mechanics and nuclear physics within a remarkably compressed period of time.

And while we’ve made meaningful discoveries in recent decades, including the Higgs boson and gravitational waves, we haven’t experienced anything comparable to that period of foundational discovery in recent decades. We still haven’t reconciled quantum mechanics with general relativity. We still don’t know what dark matter is.

The same can be said of countless other industries. Our transportation infrastructure looks remarkably similar to what it did decades ago. Construction remains incredibly labor-intensive. We still spend years developing drugs and decades building major infrastructure projects.

Our energy infrastructure, agricultural systems and manufacturing processes have certainly become more sophisticated, but in many respects, the underlying architecture of modern civilization would be perfectly recognizable to someone living half a century ago.

Outside of computing, communications and certain areas of medicine, technological progress has often felt disappointingly incremental. We were promised the future. Instead, we were forced to ring up our own bread after shopping and then got recurring subscription fees for just to use our home toaster each morning (hereinafter referred to as ‘TAAS’, or ‘Toast As A Service’).

But I increasingly feel that we are on the precipice of an extraordinary reversal of this phenomenon, and, to be honest, it’s terrifying.

I think we are overdue for a period of massive technological change, and artificial intelligence is going to be the catalyst that reshapes virtually every aspect of human civilization. We are developing a technology that could accelerate progress across virtually every scientific and technological discipline simultaneously. Physics, mathematics, biology, engineering, medicine, defense, finance. Everything.

And increasingly, I feel as though we are beginning to see glimpses of what happens when the world starts moving considerably faster than our ability to keep up with it.

According to Reuters this morning, hackers breached Cloud One, the Air Force’s cloud infrastructure that supports everything from aircraft maintenance and military logistics to personnel records. The breach was reportedly uncovered during a platform upgrade, and it remains unclear who was responsible or what sensitive information, if any, was accessed.

Just three days ago, Bloomberg reported that hackers had also breached CIA systems. The compromised system was reportedly an intelligence analysis tool used to extract insights from open-source and unclassified material belonging to the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

The CIA and the US Air Force. Within three days of each other.

Then there is the endless procession of cybersecurity breaches, infrastructure outages, service disruptions and technological failures over the past two weeks.

It feels as though we’ve seen dozens of these incidents. Every morning, I wake up to another headline about some compromised system, some major vulnerability or some piece of digital infrastructure experiencing problems. The sheer frequency of these headlines is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

Among those affected by breaches, outages or service disruptions reported in just the last three weeks are the US Air Force, the CIA, the FBI, the NSA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the US Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, the US Department of Agriculture, the Federal Aviation Administration, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Zelle, United Airlines, Anthropic, Workday, Sony’s PlayStation Network, Ticketmaster, Equinor, Visa and Mastercard, to name a few.

That is fucking insane…

Outages aren’t necessarily cyberattacks, and cyberattacks existed long before generative AI. But I am increasingly concerned about the technological environment in which all of this is occurring. We are rapidly expanding the capabilities available to offensive actors while the institutions responsible for defending against them are still operating within bureaucratic structures, procurement cycles and security frameworks designed for an entirely different technological era. The attacker gets access to a more powerful model. The defender schedules a committee meeting for next quarter.

There are also articles circulating on social media about potential breakthroughs in RSA encryption, AI systems solving longstanding mathematical problems and capabilities that would have seemed completely implausible just a few years ago.

Some of these rumors are undoubtedly exaggerated, and there is no verified basis here for declaring RSA broken. But what strikes me is how quickly the boundaries of what we consider plausible are shifting. Things I would have laughed off as science fiction several years ago are now things I feel compelled to seriously contemplate.

“I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells,” computer scientist Scott Aaronson wrote.

Several researchers say they have heard that some of the leading AI laboratories have discovered algorithms capable of breaking public-key cryptography in ‘polynomial time’ (or ‘P’ in computer-science shorthand).

It feels like the world is beginning to change at hyperspeed.

AI is no longer some abstract technological phenomenon that we spend our time theorizing about. It is here, it is proliferating, and it is taking hold at an absolutely gripping pace. And frankly, that pace scares the shit out of me.

I genuinely believe the world could be a profoundly different place one year from now.

I don’t think most people appreciate how extraordinary a statement that is. For most of our lives, the world one year into the future has been largely predictable. Technology gets marginally better, companies release new products, economies expand or contract, and life generally continues along a familiar trajectory. I am increasingly uncomfortable making that assumption about 2027.

Much of the discussion surrounding artificial intelligence still revolves around productivity improvements, corporate margins, semiconductor demand and whether AI is going to replace junior investment bankers. Meanwhile, we are potentially approaching one of the most consequential technological thresholds in human history: artificial general intelligence and, potentially thereafter, artificial superintelligence. Nobody knows exactly when, or even whether, we will cross those thresholds. But given the magnitude of the consequences, I find the relative complacency surrounding these possibilities extraordinary.

It won’t be long…the race is on.

items.title: 11 Of SPLC's Paid Hate-Group Informants Were Working For The FBI Too... And The Feds Won't Say What They Did

11 Of SPLC's Paid Hate-Group Informants Were Working For The FBI Too... And The Feds Won't Say What They Did

The Southern Poverty Law Center told a federal court in Alabama on Wednesday that at least 11 of the informants it secretly paid to infiltrate extremist groups also worked as FBI informants, and it wants the bureau's own files on every one of them.

NEW: The SPLC disclosed in a filing today that at least 11 of its informants also worked for the FBI.

The SPLC wants the FBI to search its Delta database--a database of informants--for more info on these sources. So far, the FBI has refused. And so now the SPLC is seeking a... https://t.co/IGXis1ze7T pic.twitter.com/vPDhQMmLf4

— Ken Silva (@JD_Cashless) November 25, 2026

In a status update on its motion to compel, the SPLC's lawyers asked the court to order prosecutors to "Disclose the source files from Delta for the 11 SPLC informants who also worked as FBI informants." Delta is the FBI's separate database for its confidential human sources. The list the SPLC wants runs from quarterly supervisory reviews of each source, payment requests and receipts to the FD-1023 reports of what the sources told agents, plus "any request or authorization for the informant to engage in otherwise illegal activity" and any accomplishment reports showing "Disruption or Dismantlement of an Organization."

Those files, the SPLC argues, could show that its informants "had long been providing reliable information to help dismantle extremist groups," or "that any supposedly illegal acts by the informants may have been done at the government's behest (and not the SPLC's)."

Prosecutors' own status update, filed the same day, refers to "known Fs who were also FBI CHSs at one point" - F being the SPLC's code for its informants, CHS the FBI's term for a confidential human source. But the prosecution team, they wrote, "has run no searches in Delta, other than for Giglio information for expected trial witnesses," and it isn't going to.

"Even if a person was an SPLC F and an FBI CHS, the FBI was not jointly running the source with the SPLC. The SPLC is not a law enforcement agency," First Assistant US Attorney Kevin Davidson wrote. "The information that may be in Delta has absolutely no materiality to this case."

The government says the SPLC wants the records to argue it was handing informant intelligence to law enforcement and so wasn't defrauding its donors, which prosecutors call "not relevant to any charged offense." Ordering the search would send the government on "a fishing expedition" for "highly sensitive information," Davidson wrote, when the SPLC could simply put an FBI agent on the stand to explain how the bureau oversees a source.

The court has already leaned the other way. At a Nov. 18 motions hearing it told the parties the SPLC's "request is for material information" and that "there will be an order for production of some material," according to the SPLC's filing, and gave both sides a week to narrow the searches. The SPLC says that week went nowhere: prosecutors "repeatedly claimed" the information was "sensitive" or "confidential" without naming a legal basis, and would not even list the kinds of documents in the two source files they had already obtained.

The searches prosecutors did run were in Sentinel, the FBI's main case system, covering 2007 through 2023. "SPLC" turned up in 151 FBI interview reports, known as 302s, and "Southern Poverty Law Center" in 224. The informants' real names appeared in 1,756, which prosecutors put down partly to the many informants who led extremist groups the FBI was investigating, and partly to two who share a name with FBI personnel. Paired with "SPLC," the names turned up in just seven 302s, none of which held Brady material, prosecutors said. They added that two investigations the SPLC says began with its tips were opened on information from other sources.

The SPLC has also asked what it told the FBI before and after the 2017 Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville. "Charlottesville" alone hit 3,871 interview reports; "Charlottesville AND SPLC" hit 13. A search for 14 other instances in which the SPLC says its informants cooperated with the FBI hasn't been run yet; prosecutors say they will start it Monday, Nov. 30, and won't disclose the document types it turns up.

The fight over Delta goes back to September, when a joint status report said the government had told the defense on Sept. 9 that some of the material sat in Delta and that it "does not intend to search the Delta database, for any time period." The same report said individual informants' names drew anywhere from zero to 4,197 hits in Sentinel.

The SPLC was indicted in April on 11 counts, including wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy, accused of funneling at least $3 million in donor money to at least eight informants inside the Klan, neo-Nazi groups and other extremist outfits from 2014 through 2023. Heidi Beirich, who ran its Intelligence Project until 2019, was arrested in August under a superseding indictment. Both have pleaded not guilty, and the case is headed for trial in February.

On Tuesday the court denied the SPLC's request for an order making F-9, the former informant now cooperating with prosecutors, preserve his archive: 1,800 pages of notes from his time as an SPLC informant, plus a storage unit with six steel file cabinets and about 37,000 photographs.

The SPLC's filing closes on the point it has been pressing for six months: "The Constitution requires the government to put as much effort into finding and producing exculpatory information as well."

items.title: Joe Biden's Memoir Is Full Of Easily Disproven Lies
items.content_text:
Joe Biden's Memoir Is Full Of Easily Disproven Lies

Authored by Matt Margolis via PJ Media,

Joe Biden has a long, well-documented record of fabricating and exaggerating his own biography, and he keeps repeating debunked stories as if saying them often enough could make them true.

For example, his son, Beau Biden, died of brain cancer at Walter Reed in 2015, yet Joe has repeatedly claimed that Beau "lost his life in Iraq."

And then there's another whopper he loves to tell about having an "epiphany" as a teenager that turned him into a champion of gay rights.

According to Biden, during his senior year of high school, his father dropped him off in Wilmington when they saw two men in suits kiss. "Joey, it's simple. They love each other," Biden claims his dad told him. He calls that moment the "epiphany" that shaped his views on same-sex marriage.

His actual record shows no such epiphany ever happened.

As a senator, Biden opposed letting gay people work in the federal government because he considered them a security risk. He backed "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" and voted for the Defense of Marriage Act, and even as vice president, he initially opposed civil unions for same-sex couples.

When a man spends decades lying about his past to build a political brand, it's inevitable that his presidential memoir will be full of whoppers too.

Sure enough, a Washington Free Beacon review by Jon Levine found that Promise Me, America is loaded with factual errors and embellishments.

The biggest one involves Biden's first Senate run.

In the book, Biden wrote that he was "angered by a growing pattern of lies coming out of Washington" when he ran in 1972, and he named Richard Nixon's Watergate cover-up as one reason. The problem is the chronology doesn't support this fairy tale. The Watergate break-in happened on June 17, 1972, months after Biden had launched his Delaware Senate campaign.

Biden, then 29, formally declared his candidacy in January 1972, but he was already calling himself a "candidate" in 1971, and a November 1970 profile pegged him as a Democrat hopeful for the 1972 race. The scandal didn't unravel until the spring of 1973, and by then Biden had already won and taken the oath of office.

According to the Free Beacon, its line-by-line analysis turned up enough mistakes to suggest nobody ever fact-checked the book. And I'm sure that was intentional. A review in the U.K. Observer said the book is "rather obviously written by committee," produced by the same former West Wing operation that scripted Biden's presidency.

I don't think anyone actually believes Joe Biden wrote this book. I'm sure a bunch of people worked with him and his ghostwriter to bring it all together, but clearly, Biden's insistence on putting narratives before facts remains.

Take the American Rescue Plan Act. Biden wrote that the bill cleared the Senate on March 7 with Vice President Kamala Harris casting the tie-breaking vote, which he called "the first in a record number" of her tiebreakers.

However, the Senate actually passed it on March 6, 2021, by a 50-49 margin. So final passage did not need a tiebreaker. In fact, Kamala had already cast her first tie-breaking vote back in February 2021.

What a stupid thing to get wrong. And for what?

The border section is worse, since immigration is the issue that helped send Donald Trump back to the White House.

In the memoir, Biden called the February 2024 border deal "the toughest, most effective immigration and border bill ever put together," and he wrote that it would shut down the border if "more than four thousand people a week" tried to enter.

Not true. The actual bill would have triggered a shutdown at 5,000 crossings per day, or about 35,000 per week. Biden's version inflates the bill's toughness on an issue about which he faced bipartisan criticism for inaction.

The Free Beacon also found at least a dozen misstated dates and smaller errors. Biden placed his 2020 campaign kickoff rally in Philadelphia in April 2019, for example, even though it happened in May 2019, a date the book's own endnotes get right. Sloppy. Sloppy. Sloppy.

Telling lies about your story on the campaign trail or in an interview is bad enough. But people expect a stronger commitment to accuracy in a book. We're not talking about spinning a story in a positive way; we're talking about blatant factual errors and outright lies. That lack of interest in the truth in his presidential memoir, his final attempt to shape his presidential legacy, is a reflection of the dishonesty he's demonstrated throughout his career.

Brazilian stocks surged Friday morning after socialist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva tapped Bradesco chief Luiz Carlos Trabuco as his next finance minister. Just hours after the announcement, Bradesco analysts upgraded Brazilian equities.

Gross debt is projected to rise by 8 percentage points to 86% of GDP, with another 4-percentage-point increase possible in 2027, according to Adam Goldsmith, a macroeconomic and geopolitical consultant at advisory firm Greenmantle.

Trabuco faces a major challenge next year: restoring fiscal credibility while serving a socialist president whose spending promises threaten to push the South American country's debt burden even higher.

Bradesco chief Luiz Carlos Trabuco

EWZ Roller Coaster

items.title: "This Is Not The End Of It": Democrats Plot To Defund Iran War, Impeach Hegseth, Gut Trump's $1.5 Trillion Defense Budget
items.content_text:
"This Is Not The End Of It": Democrats Plot To Defund Iran War, Impeach Hegseth, Gut Trump's $1.5 Trillion Defense Budget

Authored by Ryan Morgan via The Epoch Times,

Having won both houses of Congress amid popular opposition to the war in Iran, Democratic lawmakers are positioned to impose a substantial check on President Donald Trump's military and foreign policy agenda over the next two years.

The Iran conflict precipitated disruptions to Middle Eastern trade routes, driving up fuel prices around the world. This, in turn, led to the Democrats shaping much of their midterm messaging around affordability angst to secure 56 Senate seats and at least 257 House seats.

Though Democrats won't officially take control of the House and Senate until Jan. 3, they have already announced efforts to constrain Trump's use of the military abroad before the new term. They have also called for expansive oversight investigations after they gain subpoena power in the new year.

With the power to appropriate funds and confirm nominees in Democrats' hands, Trump will face tougher odds for advancing his agenda.

Military, Foreign Policy Facing Oversight

Democratic lawmakers have vowed to conduct investigations and hold impeachment proceedings targeting various Trump administration officials.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has become a top target for impeachment as Democrats prepare to take controlling majorities in both chambers of Congress.

During the lame-duck period, the Republican-led House of Representatives effectively blocked one impeachment effort, brought by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.). On Nov. 10, the House voted 211-204 to refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, where it's unlikely to advance in the time remaining.

Following the vote, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told reporters: "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning."

Hans von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, told The Epoch Times that Democrats will likely move forward with the impeachment process against Hegseth and target other Trump administration officials once they take control in January.

"They're interested in revenge against anyone and everyone who has served in the Trump administration," he said.

Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the current ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, said that the top priority of the committee under Democratic leadership will be "vigorous oversight of the Department of Defense and the Trump Administration."

House Intelligence Committee Ranking Member Jim Himes (D-Conn.) said earlier this month that Democrats are planning to investigate various U.S. intelligence community operations, such as staff reductions and the use of covert operations.

Democratic lawmakers have also signaled plans to investigate the U.S. military's lethal strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats and land operations in the Caribbean and Latin America.

Democrats could also investigate the Pentagon's leadership and culture changes implemented under Hegseth.

Asked how holding hearings and launching investigations would lower costs for Americans, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told reporters, "If you have people in who got us into this illegal, immoral war in Iran, and you try to wind down that war, that can lower gas prices, diesel prices, [and] food prices."

Democrats Navigating Iran War Exit

Halting the armed standoff with Iran remains a hot-button issue for the Democrats and their base of support, but the party hasn't yet decided how best to go about it.

Some Democrats are pushing to halt the Middle East conflict even before January by taking advantage of a Dec. 11 funding deadline.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the title of majority leader come Jan. 3, has said he will not support a government funding bill "unless it defunds this war."

Sens. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) have sponsored language for an amendment to any government funding bill, to block the use of funds for offensive military operations against Iran. At a Nov. 19 news conference announcing the amendment, Duckworth said her plan would allow funding to continue for defensive military operations in the Middle East, as well as continuing efforts to de-mine the Strait of Hormuz and provide military escorts for commercial ships seeking to transit that key waterway.

Even if Democrats can pass legislation to halt funding for offensive operations, the Trump administration may be able to continue such operations using previously appropriated funds.

Asked about that possibility, Duckworth said, "We will deal with that when we get into next year."

Duckworth said consultations were ongoing with Democrats to prepare a House companion amendment.

Smith expressed reservations about using the appropriations deadline to force a hard cutoff in funding for Iran-related operations.

"The president should end the war. But if we cut off all funding, what does that do to the 50,000 service members who are in the region?" he told The Epoch Times on Nov. 19. "They're already being stretched beyond where they should be. So yeah, we're trying to figure out how to do that."

Asked what would be an appropriate conclusion to the Iran conflict, Smith said he was still consulting with his team to make that determination.

Zelenskyy Buoyed by US Political Shift

The shift of power in Washington could also affect aid for Ukraine amid the Trump administration's push for a peace deal between Moscow and Kyiv.

"Our chances of receiving additional assistance from the United States of America may now increase," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Nov. 5 interview for United News.

Democratic aides in both the House and Senate have signaled that strengthening U.S. support for Ukraine will be a top priority under Democratic majorities.

Congress has not passed major Ukraine aid legislation since the start of Trump's second administration last year.

"The Trump administration has been coy in committing to these life-saving funds in Ukraine and the sooner that changes the better," Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), who serves on the Senate Appropriations Committee, told Reuters.

Trump has repeatedly called for Russia and Ukraine to reach a deal to end the war, which has now lasted more than 4 1/2 years.

The United States, earlier this month, held trilateral peace talks with Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.

Nominees Face Headwinds

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, Trump's Navy secretary nominee, was grilled by Senate Democrats during his confirmation hearing on Nov. 17.

To be confirmed by the Senate, Cao would need both the House and the Senate to approve a waiver because of federal law requiring former U.S. military officers to wait seven years before serving as service secretaries. He retired from the Navy in 2021.

Cao's waiver would need approval from all 53 Republican senators and at least seven Democratic senators to reach the 60-vote filibuster threshold.

During the confirmation hearing, Duckworth repeatedly asked Cao whether he had stood up to Hegseth in opposition to continued military operations in Iran. When Cao told Duckworth that it was not within his purview to do that, the senator said, "I cannot vote for you because you're going to be another yes-man."

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, also signaled potential opposition to Cao.

"I have serious questions about your decision-making, about your willingness to stand up to your superiors and make clear your views and that they should be listened to, and about your ability to be transparent with Congress," she said.

Trump may face a tough time advancing other nominees through the confirmation process.

He is looking to have Daniel Zimmerman approved for the newly created role of assistant secretary of War for international armaments cooperation.

The Department of the Army lacks a Senate-confirmed leader. The Army also needs a Senate-confirmed uniformed chief of staff.

Additionally, nearly half of the 196 slots for U.S. ambassadorships around the world remain vacant.

Any military and foreign service nominees hoping to advance while the Senate is still under Republican control will have to compete for attention with judicial nominees also seeking advancement.

Budget Cuts Could Curtail Military Projects

Democrats could also weigh on Trump's push for his proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget request for 2027.

Trump had sought about $1.1 trillion of that ask through a primary appropriation, with another $350 billion through a reconciliation bill. Several Democrats have cast doubt on the request.

"We must push for the development of a more realistic and sustainable approach to our national security - one that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or one paid for with draconian cuts to critical domestic programs," Smith said in a statement the day after the 2026 midterm elections.

Speaking at a Hudson Institute conference on Nov. 18, Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Ala.), chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, said that the $350 billion reconciliation plan won't happen but that a smaller reconciliation may still be possible.

"If they can skinny that reconciliation from 350 down to 100 or somewhere in that nature, there is a path for that," Rogers said.

With faltering support for his full 2027 budget request, Trump will likely have to reshape plans for military projects he has sought, such as the Golden Dome for America missile and air defense initiative and a proposed nuclear-powered Trump-class battleship.

Trump's 2027 military budget calls for a $17.5 billion investment in Golden Dome. About $17 billion of that funding comes through the requested reconciliation bill.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, told The Epoch Times that he believes that there will be continuing bipartisan support for Golden Dome but that the scope of the project would likely change.

Kaine said Canadian buy-in to the Golden Dome project would also improve its feasibility. He said improving U.S.-Canada relations would make their participation more likely, but criticized Trump for straining those ties with tariffs.

"I think the notion of a better continental missile defense system is something the Democrats will broadly support," Kaine said. "We just want to make sure that we're doing it the right way."

The Virginia Democrat was less certain about the future of the battleship.

"I haven't heard, necessarily, what I would consider really good military justification for [the Trump-class battleship]. Contrary to the missile defense, where there is a good justification," he said.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.), a member of the House Armed Services Committee's Subcommittee on Sea Power and Projection Forces, outright dismissed the Trump-class battleship.

"It's not going to happen. It's not going to be a ship that's built in this country," Deluzio told The Epoch Times.

items.title: Washington Quietly Preparing To Automatically Register Millions Of Men For Military Draft
items.content_text:
Washington Quietly Preparing To Automatically Register Millions Of Men For Military Draft

The U.S. government is preparing to fundamentally overhaul its military draft registration system in December, automatically enrolling eligible young men in a federal database that could be used to mobilize Americans in the event of a national emergency, the Center on Conscience & War reports.

The move marks a significant departure from the decades-old system that requires men to register with the Selective Service System themselves.

Under a provision tucked into the fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, which President Donald Trump signed into law last December, American men between the ages of 18 and 25 will no longer have to manually register. Instead, Washington will assume responsibility for their enrollment, according to an April report from Stars & Stripes.

The Selective Service System will tap existing government databases to identify eligible men, effectively eliminating the need for individuals to submit their personal information.

The agency previously described the overhaul as a "streamlined registration process and corresponding workforce realignment."

Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE), a proponent of automatic registration, co-introduced the measure with Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-PA).

Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-PA), who helped spearhead the automatic registration legislation, stressed in a June 2024 statement that the measure "does not reinstate the draft" and that neither chamber of Congress was considering such a move at the time.

"I want to set the record straight: Since 1917, men aged 18 to 25 have been required to register with the Selective Service. This new legislation saves taxpayers significant money and makes it easier for these men to follow the law and register with the Selective Service. That is all. Full stop," Houlahan said in a statement.

"This legislation does not reinstate the draft. Reinstating the draft would require a separate act by Congress that would have to pass both the U.S. House and Senate and be signed into law by the President," the House Democrat added. "This idea is not currently being weighed in either chamber. Our nation has not had a military draft in more than a half-century, and I spend a great deal of my time in Congress working to ensure that we never will again."

However, with the December 18 statutory deadline fast approaching, questions remain over how the federal government intends to roll out the system. The proposed regulation governing its implementation was withdrawn earlier this year, and a replacement has yet to be publicly unveiled.

The U.S. has not conducted a military draft since 1973, when it transitioned to an all-volunteer fighting force. President Jimmy Carter reinstated mandatory registration in 1980 amid escalating Cold War tensions.

More than 50 peace, religious and civil liberties organizations have joined forces to oppose automatic draft registration and demand the repeal of the Military Selective Service Act.

Edward Hasbrouck, an organizer of the Anti-Draft Coalition, which is calling for the repeal of the Military Selective Service Act, has warned that automatic registration amounts to a "really dangerous data grab."

"I think it's interesting, in Congress, even though support for continuing draft registration or expanding it or trying to salvage it from failure has been bipartisan, the opposition has also been bipartisan," Hasbrouck told the New York Post in April. "In order to attempt to register people automatically, the Selective Service System will be given unprecedented authority to access databases of any other federal agency that it thinks might help identify or locate potential draftees."

items.title: Democrats On Warpath Have Fresh Ammo Against Nvidia As Two 'American' Customers Answer To Chinese Owners
items.content_text:
Democrats On Warpath Have Fresh Ammo Against Nvidia As Two 'American' Customers Answer To Chinese Owners

Democrats who take the gavels in both chambers of Congress in January already have Nvidia in their sights, and a new CBS News investigation just handed them more. Nvidia has been selling advanced AI chips to at least two California companies controlled by Chinese-owned parents and classifying them as American customers. One is headed by a graduate of a Chinese military university. The other kept its "elite" Nvidia partner status after related Chinese entities were blacklisted, simply by changing its name.

On Nov. 12, hours after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO (he has since returned), Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Richard Neal, the top Democrats on Senate Finance and House Ways and Means, opened an investigation into Nvidia chip exports to Chinese companies "with concerning links to the Chinese government, military, and sanctioned entities." Sen. Elizabeth Warren has said Nvidia's board owes Congress answers. And Sen. Chris Coons, who has pressed Commerce on Nvidia's China sales for months, takes over the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Jan. 3.

For the market's most crowded trade, the timing could hardly be worse. The report lands days after the Commerce Department blacklisted Megaspeed, the Singapore firm where Alice Huang - the woman at the center of the Jensen Huang saga - was a senior executive. The Justice Department has not concluded whether she is a spy. The US government has not accused RiCloud AI or its parent Yuxing InfoTech of wrongdoing.

Partner Status In Ten Weeks

San Jose-based RiCloud AI had secured Nvidia partner status by December 2025, roughly ten weeks after it was incorporated, and has since become a preferred partner, with priority access to advanced chips and support. Nvidia counts sales to the firm as US revenue in its annual filing.

RiCloud's parent, Shenzhen-based Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings, is listed in Hong Kong. Its CEO and co-owner, Cong Yu, holds a degree in National Defense Mobilization from the People's Liberation Army Command College, according to Yuxing's own Hong Kong filing. Yuxing's chairman, Li Qiang, previously chaired Global Switch Holdings, which Australia's Department of Defence dropped in June 2024 over national-security concerns.

One RiCloud customer is Agencia Comercial Spirits, a Taiwanese whisky importer that reported $609,000 in net income in 2025 before listing on Nasdaq as an AI company. In January it signed a letter of intent to lease about 300 Nvidia B300 servers from RiCloud for an estimated $120 million. After Li Qiang became its chairman, Agencia committed to AI data-center deals worth $488 million to $598 million this year.

Rebrand After Blacklist

Aivres, listed at Nvidia's highest elite partner tier, used to operate under the Inspur name. When Inspur-related firms in China were added to the US Entity List in March 2023, the California subsidiary dropped the name and kept the relationship. Aivres itself is not on the blacklist, though US government records say servers owned by Inspur are used by China's military, according to a Federal Register notice.

A New York Times analysis of trade records found that Aivres exported at least $5.6 billion of advanced technology to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February 2026, including roughly $3 billion in computers carrying Nvidia's restricted Blackwell chips. The servers went to two companies in Malaysia, Megaspeed and Aolani, which provided cloud AI services to Alibaba and ByteDance.

Other Partner Links

A third elite partner, the US arm of French server maker 2CRSi, is linked in records CBS reviewed to California businessman Greg Lui, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of routing more than $300 million in export-controlled servers to China via Malaysia and Singapore. 2CRSi told shareholders this month in a letter that it received a grand jury subpoena concerning a customer it had itself reported to authorities. 2CRSi has not been accused of wrongdoing, and the indictment does not accuse Nvidia of knowing about the arrangement. Lui also listed Super Micro Computer as a customer; in March the Justice Department charged Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw in an alleged $2.5 billion server-smuggling scheme, which he denies.

The "American Customer" Loophole

After Nvidia switched from reporting sales by billing location to the customer's headquarters location, the change showed an additional $7.9 billion of 2024 billings came from firms headquartered in China. Nvidia's filings note that the end customer and shipping location may differ from the customer's headquarters. Under that method, a San Jose company owned by a Shenzhen firm is classified as an American customer.

Democrats will drive the push, but they may get some Republican help: three House GOP committee chairs have already asked Huang for a closed-door briefing on his contacts with Alice Huang and Nvidia's safeguards against espionage, and have since threatened a subpoena. Sen. Jim Banks wants Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify on the "glaring mistakes" that kept Megaspeed off the export blacklist, and he wrote the GAIN Act with Warren to put American buyers ahead of China for Nvidia's advanced chips. Coons' own bill to bar the President from approving advanced AI chip sales to China, the SAFE Chips Act, was written with Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts.

With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, the San Jose mailbox loophole - and the allegations swirling around Nvidia - are about to get a lot more airtime.

"You Might Not Have This War": Trump Says Putin Is Welcome At His Doral G20, Blames Obama

"All we do is talk about Russia..."

President Trump said Thursday that Vladimir Putin "certainly can" come to next month's G20 summit at Trump's own Doral resort near Miami, and blamed Barack Obama's push to throw Russia out of the G8 for the war in Ukraine.

"I don't know, but if he wanted to come, he certainly can. Some people wouldn't like that," Trump told reporters at Mar-a-Lago on Thanksgiving, when asked whether he expected the Russian leader at the Dec. 14-15 summit.

Q: Do you expect Putin to come here for the G20 Summit at Doral?

"I don't know, but if he wanted to come, he certainly can... To be honest with you, all we do is talk about Russia. I say, 'Why isn't he here?'" pic.twitter.com/qYsXYR4PEf

— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) November 27, 2026

Trump then went back to 2014, when Russia was suspended from the G8 after annexing Crimea. "You know, when he was a member of the G8, if he stayed a member, President Obama wanted him out. And if he stayed a member, you might not have this war right now," he said. "He was very insulted when that happened. And now it's a G7."

"To be honest with you, all we do is talk about Russia. I say, why isn't he here?" Trump continued, adding that Obama, Canada, the US "and I guess a couple of others" had voted Russia out. "I wouldn't have voted that way. I would say that if it were up to me, I'd like to have him. I thought it was a much more powerful group when you had Russia that you're talking about."

Earlier Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that "the president has not yet made a decision on attending the G20 summit in Miami." Peskov told Izvestia the same on Tuesday, and on Nov. 18 he said the call would turn in part on how Putin's talks with Trump in Shenzhen went.

Those talks ended in the first-ever summit of the US, Chinese and Russian leaders and a four-point "Declaration Toward Peace," as we reported. Trump said Thursday he came away convinced Putin wants the war over: "I think Putin would like to see the war end. I believe that. It takes two to tango, but I believe he wants to see it end. I think the other side wants to see it end. I can tell you NATO would like to see it end."

.@POTUS: "I think Putin would like to see the war end. I believe that. It takes two to tango, but I believe he wants to see it end. I think the other side wants to see it end. I can tell you NATO would like to see it end." https://t.co/tlupDO80uq pic.twitter.com/IQof5ZyKBC

— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) November 26, 2026

The remarks came a day after Trump hosted NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at Mar-a-Lago, where the two warned Moscow against "any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio put the invitation on the table in September: "We've invited President Putin to the G20. We hope that's an invitation he'll accept." The Kremlin answered that it was "grateful for and appreciative of this invitation," days after Bloomberg reported that the chance of Putin joining Trump in Florida was "very slim."

Fourteen senators from both parties, among them Republicans Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn, Roger Wicker and Thom Tillis alongside Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, urged Trump in September to rescind it. They cited public reports that Russia is helping Iran's military target American service members in the Middle East, and asked: "what incentive does Russia have to agree to a ceasefire?"

Putin has not attended a G20 summit in person since Osaka in 2019. This year's gathering will be short a member either way: Trump said South Africa won't be invited.

items.title: Hochul Bans AI Chatbot Toys For 5 Years After Tests Found Them Talking Sex With Kids
items.content_text:
Hochul Bans AI Chatbot Toys For 5 Years After Tests Found Them Talking Sex With Kids

Authored by Chris Wade via The Center Square,

Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a bill Tuesday setting a temporary ban on artificial intelligence-powered chatbot toys, less than a day after videoing a bill requiring warning labels on AI products.

The legislation signed by the governor Tuesday sets a five-year ban on toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots - including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to communicate with children. The measure goes into effect in 90 days, meaning it won't affect toys in the upcoming holiday season.

But Hochul warned parents to be cautious in purchasing those items. She cited reports by a national consumer watchdog that said tests of some AI chatbot toys marketed to young children revealed the devices engaged in sexually explicit conversations, among other issues.

"Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk," Hochul said Tuesday.

Parents have enough to worry about without wondering whether the teddy bear they bought their child is safe.⁰⁰And when AI threatens the safety of our kids, you can bet I'm going to do something about it.⁰⁰Today, I took action to protect our children from dangerous AI chatbots... pic.twitter.com/VNoLozWbEd

— Governor Kathy Hochul (@GovKathyHochul) November 24, 2026

The new law empowers the New York Attorney General's Office to enforce the law and violators face civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for every violation.

But the governor's approval of the chatbot ban comes after she vetoed another bill that would have required the owners, operators or licensees of a generative AI platform to "clearly and conspicuously" display a notice on the system's user interface warning that information provided by the system "may be inaccurate."

But Hochul said that bill would likely run afoul of First Amendment rights because it "takes an inflexible one-size-fits-all approach to require notifications on all generative Al systems regardless of context and in doing so, the bill may present constitutional and pragmatic challenges." That would leave the state, and its taxpayers, open to a legal challenge, she said.

Neither of the bill's primary sponsors, state Assembly member Clyde Vanel and state Sen. Kirsten Gonzalez, immediately responded to requests for comment from The Center Square. The Queens Democrats filed the bill last year after Meta's AI platform made false sexual-harassment allegations against a number of New York lawmakers.

Even if lawmakers re-write the bill to address Hochul's concerns, it would have to wait until the next legislative session that gets underway in January.

Hochul hasn't proposed an alternative to the disclaimer bill, and her office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

But the two-term governor, who won another full term in the Nov. 3 election, has taken aim at big tech companies over the rapid development of AI platforms despite threats of legal challenges from the industry and a lack of support from the federal government.

In October, Hochul signed legislation prohibiting companies from offering certain unsafe AI chatbot features to minors, including those that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage children in sexually explicit conversations.

Under the Responsible AI Safety and Education, or RAISE Act, which goes into effect in January, new state-level transparency, safety, and reporting requirements will be set for developers of the most AI models. The new law requires AI companies to register with the state by the end of November and report any critical safety incidents within 72 hours.

Another bill awaiting action by Hochul would set a long-term moratorium on data centers that lawmakers approved earlier this year. Hochul has until Dec. 31 to sign, veto or send the measure.

items.title: Hundreds Of Thousands Still In The Dark After Brutal Thanksgiving Storm, And Another One Is Coming
items.content_text:
Hundreds Of Thousands Still In The Dark After Brutal Thanksgiving Storm, And Another One Is Coming

More than 600,000 homes and businesses across the Midwest and East Coast were still without power Friday morning, after a Thanksgiving storm of wind, flooding rain and heavy snow knocked out electricity to close to one million customers at its peak Thursday night, according to PowerOutage.us.

Pennsylvania had the most customers out Friday morning, about 149,000, followed by New Jersey with more than 129,000 and Maryland with 88,000. Utilities from Virginia to Missouri are warning that getting the rest back will take days, not hours.

Heavy, wet snow brought down lines across the St. Louis metro area, where Ameren Missouri said about 123,000 households and businesses were without power as of 9 a.m. Thursday, across more than 4,300 separate outages. The utility said restoration "is expected to take multiple days" and has called in mutual-aid crews from outside the region. St. Louis recorded 7.3 inches of snow, Ste. Genevieve 14 inches and French Village 15.

Dominion Energy called its own cleanup in Virginia "a multi-day restoration effort," citing broken poles and large trees down on wires. Outside Philadelphia, PECO's outage map showed 61,491 customers out late Thursday, more than half of them in Chester County, FOX 29 reported; that had fallen to about 39,000 by early Friday.

In the Washington suburbs, the blackouts reached the tap. WSSC Water told all 1.9 million of its customers in Montgomery and Prince George's counties to use water only when necessary after storm-related power disruptions hit its filtration plants. Its Potomac plant had power but kept suffering interruptions, while its Patuxent plant, already offline for planned maintenance, lost power as well. The utility asked customers to take shorter showers, limit toilet flushing and hold off on washing machines and dishwashers, while saying the water "remains safe to drink." It is the same Potomac plant whose electrical problems forced a similar order in late September.

On the Jersey Shore, Avalon saw some of the worst flooding in its history, and the borough's administrator, Scott J. Wahl, put it at "Not quite Hurricane Sandy." US Route 30 into Atlantic City was closed in both directions, and Cape May matched its record tide of 9.41 feet while Wachapreague, Virginia, hit 9.94 feet. In North Carolina, seawater breached the dunes and closed NC 12, the only highway linking Hatteras Island to the mainland, after Emerald Isle took 9.16 inches of rain.

Central Park logged 1.82 inches of rain, making it New York City's wettest Thanksgiving on record and topping the 1.72 inches set in 2006, and LaGuardia clocked a 56 mph gust. 

Mayor Zohran Mamdani said two people were rescued from their cars in floodwater, and Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for parts of the state, as New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill did statewide.

Central Park has picked up 1.82" of rain so far today, making this the wettest Thanksgiving on record at the site.

The previous record was 1.72", set on Nov 23, 2006. All data preliminary.https://t.co/5Hpao2usRD

— NWS New York NY (@NWSNewYorkNY) November 27, 2026

items.title: Why Knot?
items.content_text:
Why Knot?

By Bas van Geffen, senior macro strategist of Rabobank

De Cos they said so. European leaders have selected the former head of the Spanish central bank to replace ECB president Lagarde over his Dutch peer.

De Cos’ nomination is a deal in which German economist Brunnermeier and French economist Laurence Boone will both get a seat at the table as well. Staff changes will happen over a matter of months starting in January, when Schnabel makes place for Boone. 

The Spanish candidate is generally seen as leaning less hawkish than Klaas Knot, but arguably the German pick for Brunnermeier is the more interesting one. Brunnermeier is not the traditional Bundesbank hawk. In fact, he was one of the proponents of a plan to create Eurozone-wide safe assets, the so-called ESBies. 

Contrast that to current German member of the Executive Board. Isabel Schnabel has been one of the more hawkish policymakers at the central bank. So, Brunnermeier could mark a change in tone. But the German has also expressed caution about inflation signals and the impact of QE. So, it may take a crisis –or at least some very difficult policy choices– to reveal the latent preferences of the new leadership. 

And the new team will probably get tested sooner than later: De Cos will be installed before the French presidential elections. Meanwhile, the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine continue to cast doubt over the outlook for energy markets, inflation and growth; and this month’s wobbles in the AI trade add to concerns that the AI-driven investment boom might not support economic activity as much in the coming year as it has done over the past quarters.

Because it has been a bit of a Black Friday sale in tech stocks this week. The reinstatement of Jensen Huang at NVIDIA created some support for the sector, but it did not convincingly turn the fortunes of AI-related stocks. The Nasdaq is currently 3.8% still discounted from last Friday’s close, or about -8% month-to-date. Will buyers try to find a bargain today? Are they waiting for Cyber Monday?

New export controls are certainly not helping the mood. NVIDIA halted shipments to Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia as the US administration tightens controls to prevent that the most powerful AI chips end up in Chinese hands. However, limited access to US chip technology only pushes China to advance its own semiconductor industry. Huawei is reportedly making progress on its own chip design and production infrastructure.

The new restrictions could also create new friction between Washington and Europe. The MATCH Act would require other countries to tighten their export controls in tandem with the US. The Dutch government is trying to prevent the bill from passing and will seek to limit the consequences if US Congress does vote in favour of the bill. 

Theoretically, the European Union could invoke its Blocking Statute and/or Anti-Coercion Tool to prohibit companies from complying with foreign rules. However, that is bound to trigger a new trade dispute with the US. Moreover, Brussels would risk losing the US defence umbrella. So, the EU may seek to employ less confrontational means first.

Delayed delivery of US anti-ballistic missiles is already making Ukraine’s defence more difficult, as the country prepares for another round of large-scale missile strikes. European Council President Costa said that 24 EU member states support a new €45 billion loan to Ukraine, but money alone doesn’t win a war. 

At the same time, some European leaders are increasingly concerned that the conflict could broaden. Italy’s Meloni rebuked Ukraine’s attacks on a Russian warship at a Libyan naval base, concerned that the war could spread from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean. Between this and Trump telling Ukraine to stop targeting Russian refineries earlier, that would leave few options for the country to exert counterpressure on its aggressor. 

And the EU members again failed to reach a consensus on Brussels’ multi-annual budget. Meloni said that the countries are still “light years away” from any agreement, as the huge costs of Europe’s security and industrial challenges are difficult to reconcile with strained public finances, and low political will to make concessions ahead of an election cycle across the continent.

So, there probably won’t be much time for an induction for De Cos and his new colleagues. And the accounts of the October ECB meeting still leave all options open for the new leadership. The write-up of the previous policy meeting provided some strong hints that a rate hike is indeed forthcoming in December – as widely expected by markets: “A large number of policymakers […] could have supported raising interest rates” in October already.

However, the accounts provide less direction for policy rates in 2027. Hawkishly, there were some concerns that inflation could only return to target after 2028, and policymakers noted that inflation data suggested that the risk of an overshoot had worsened. But on the dovish side, members argued that there were no indications of second-round effects, with wages showing no material response at this stage. 

Today’s French and Spanish inflation data supports a more cautious approach. Headline inflation came in significantly below expectations in both countries as energy price pressures eased. Moreover, Spain’s core HICP decelerated significantly from 3.1% to 2.6% this month. At the same time, a downward revision of French Q3 GDP growth from -0.1% to 0.2% q/q underscores that the economic resilience to shocks is finite.

In Fiery Video Of Chaos And Destruction, Iran State Media Warns Amazon, Microsoft And SpaceX: "Repent" Or Face Consequences

Iran's state-sponsored Mehr News Agency marked Thanksgiving with an AI-generated video of drones blowing up the headquarters of Amazon, Microsoft and Elon Musk's SpaceX, and a narrator warning that "the companies that took part in the attack on Iran will either pay reparations and repent or face destruction on the same scale."

Mehr, which is based in Tehran, posted the video on its Telegram channel Thursday afternoon, as the Daily Mail first reported. It also threatens the governments of the US and Israel. "We won't let the killers of our children off the hook," the narrator says as the attack begins, then adds: "We will not harm the American people."

"Consider this a warning," the video goes on, as the buildings burn under the drones. It closes on a question: "Repentance or destruction? The choice is yours, America."

The Persian caption Mehr posted with it ties the threat to Minab: "A stern warning to companies complicit in crimes against the Iranian people and the innocent children of Minab!" (translated) "From Amazon to Microsoft, companies that have secret collaborations with US and Israeli military units cannot escape accountability" (translated).

Minab is the southern Iranian town where a Tomahawk strike on Feb. 28, the first day of the war, hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school. The local prosecutor put the final toll at 156, most of them children, and the Pentagon's own investigation pinned the strike on US forces, blaming flawed intelligence, outdated imagery and an overreliance on AI. As we reported last month, Hegseth's advisers planned to withhold the report until after the midterms.

Reparations are one of the seven conditions Tehran has set for ending the war for good, and this week Hassan Abdolianpour, who heads the Iranian judiciary's center for lawyers, said Iranian courts had awarded $290 billion in damages against the US.

US tech firms have been on Iran's target list since the opening days of the war. In early March IRGC drones hit two Amazon Web Services data centers in the UAE, and Iranian state media claimed strikes on Microsoft data centers in the Gulf; the Guards later threatened the "complete and utter annihilation" of OpenAI's Stargate site in Abu Dhabi. Thursday's video goes further, putting the companies' American headquarters in the crosshairs rather than their Gulf server farms.

Trump told Fox News on Sunday that he is ready to strike Iran again after the new year if no deal is reached, calling Iran's negotiators "professional tap dancers," and dared Tehran to run tankers through the US blockade of Hormuz: "they'll all be at the bottom of the sea." This week an Iranian drone attack on Kuwait killed two Italian engineers working for Rheinmetall, and three tankers were set ablaze in the Strait.

Trump spent his own Thanksgiving taking calls from service members abroad. When one asked how he was spending the holiday, he answered: "Well, I'll tell you what. I'm working on a little project. It's called Iran."

Lights Out In Putin's Crimea... And Zelensky Says Russia's Next Massive Strike Is Coming

A blackout swept Russian-occupied Crimea on Thursday, and Sevastopol lost power while parts of Kerch were left without heat, ten days after Ukrainian drones and missiles brought down part of the Kerch Bridge, the peninsula's road and rail link to Russia.

Krymenergo, the Russian-controlled utility, blamed an accident at energy facilities outside the peninsula, without naming the facility or saying when power would come back, the Kyiv Post reported. It warned that outages could last up to 12 hours. Sevastopolenergo said separately that Sevastopol had lost electricity, and restrictions hit dozens of settlements, including Simferopol, Yevpatoria, Alushta and Kerch.

Trams stopped in Yevpatoria when their overhead lines lost voltage, and buses replaced trolleybuses on some routes in Simferopol.

On Nov. 24 Sergei Aksyonov, the peninsula's Russian-installed head, announced that Crimea's daytime power supply would be cut by about 30% for up to 10 days, starting the next day, while heating, water and other essential services kept running. Sevastopol's supply had already been too short to keep its scheduled rotating outages going, according to the city's utility.

Thursday's outage is the latest in a run of them since late October, when a blackout followed drone attacks on Crimea's energy infrastructure. The pressure on the peninsula has grown since Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge on Nov. 17, which Zelensky called an "unprecedented operation." The bridge was hit for the third time in a week two days later, and Moscow vowed to restore it.

In Kyiv the same day, Zelensky warned after a coordination call on Ukraine's own grid that Moscow is nearly ready to hit back. "Unfortunately, the Russians are already completing preparations for a new massive strike," he wrote on X. "According to intelligence, energy facilities and logistics infrastructure, as well as essential services facilities in cities and communities, will once again be the targets."

I held a coordination call. First of all, I want to thank all the repair crews, everyone working for energy companies, utility services, and the State Emergency Service of Ukraine who are doing their jobs truly effectively and restoring electricity supplies after Russian strikes.... pic.twitter.com/U02qKx1WD9

— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) November 26, 2026

The global story this morning is a relief rally in everything AI after weeks of anxiety: Nasdaq 100 futures are extending Wednesday's recovery, Asian tech surged led by Korea and China (see "China's National Team Sparks A 15% Rip") China's National Team Sparks A 15%, and European chip names are up for a second day, while investors rotate back out of bonds, reversing the haven trade that dominated earlier in the week. And with gold, silver and copper all ripping alongside equities, the "markets doing what they're not supposed to" award goes to a cross-asset tape where stocks, metals, oil and yields are all rising at once. As we noted yesterday, the Nasdaq narrowly dodged a bear market; today's bounce comes as Goldman's Rich Privorotsky fears AI is becoming self-cheapening.

Some of the fuel looks technical, according to Bloomberg, the Nasdaq 100 flushed below 25,000 on Wednesday before reversing to close near the top of its range, and momentum indicators remain deeply oversold, leaving room for a short-term bounce even as the broader trend stays weak.

“The rebound can have some staying power after such a sharp correction, but the burden of proof has clearly increased,” said Santiago Mateo at CaixaBank AM. “The debate is moving from AI adoption to AI economics: whether the extraordinary amount of capital being deployed can generate adequate returns.”

JPMorgan's quant team says its Global Equity Sentiment Indicator is at depressed levels that fundamentals don't yet justify, and strategists including Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou expect AI stocks to recover over the next two months, helped by depressed positioning and continued retail buying, comparing the collapse in breadth and depth to the April 2025 tariff capitulation and the pandemic. The longer-term picture is less rosy: JPM warns slower growth is being masked by strong PMIs, EPS revisions have peaked, and if upgrades keep fading markets could drift to new lows with defensives back in charge.

Mizuho's Evelyne Gomez-Liechti says that if equities keep stabilizing while oil holds its premium, yields have room to consolidate higher, though a break above 5% on the 10Y would probably require either another oil shock or a more durable improvement in risk appetite. CGS International's Angela Cheng is less convinced, telling Bloomberg TV that investors still need to be very cautious since this is likely not the bottom, even if she is optimistic on tech and China.

On the credit side, Bloomberg echoes what we first reported, noting that the gap between Nvidia's equity volatility and its CDS, flagged back in August, has finally closed, with the stock's implied vol catching up to credit about four months late.

Goldman's Rich Privorotsky opens his morning note with Asia, where Beijing finally hit its pain point: domestic stocks had sunk to a 16-month low before the State Council called for a bigger role for Central Huijin, sending the CSI 300 up almost 4%, with copper and gold back on the bid. He points to the reason Beijing may be nervous: consumer loans including mortgages fell by Rmb1.6tn in the first nine months, more than 3x the decline in all of 2025, and mortgage balances are 8% below their 2023 peak. In the US, he says 7,000 on the S&P was the line in the sand: the index fell to 6,970 on Wednesday before closing at 7,183, sentiment is washed out (fear/greed at 15, the Bull/Bear spread at -8, index puts outnumbering calls, VIX near 28), and from here he thinks vol compression can lead spot, with rich December premium giving overwriters a reason to put gamma back into the street; lower vol helps spot, and firmer spot helps vol come in.

On AI, Privorotsky is tactically bullish but has long-term questions he would love to see falsified. The Street models AI efficiency gains as gradual, he argues, yet the evidence suggests running models became roughly 3x to 15x cheaper and faster over the past year, and smarter AI writes leaner code, making the technology self-cheapening. He compares it uncomfortably to telecom in 2000, when traffic exploded as forecast but fiber tech multiplied capacity, bandwidth prices collapsed and the cable-layers got crushed: the danger is not that people stop using AI, it's that compute gets so cheap so fast that data-center capex fails to earn its return, and for Jevons Paradox to save infrastructure ROIC, demand elasticity must exceed the pace of unit-cost deflation. On China chips, he flags the new BIS licensing rule for overseas compute serving Chinese firms, Nvidia telling partners to halt server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, and Asian neoclouds shopping B300 capacity once earmarked for China to Western buyers (as we discussed earlier this week); a shift to issuing permits and a more realpolitik stance could do a lot for sentiment. His key tell: AI CDS widened even as stocks got their relief rally, so he is watching broader credit to see whether the bounce has legs; meanwhile levels have held, so let vol compress and let the systematics buy, and the market can overshoot to the upside even with every structural AI worry intact.

Elsewhere at Goldman, Jonathan Luey on the EU vol desk sees a tradeable low around 7,000 on the S&P, after the SPX and NDX retested and bounced off last Friday's panic lows; reclaiming the 200dma near 7,350 would trigger CTA covering and flip dealers flat or long gamma, which he says would go a long way toward healing the tape. Goldman's CTA models show the trend followers max short the Nasdaq 100 and Russell 2000, with first buy triggers about 3% above spot, although a Goldman estimate predating the bounce said systematic investors still had roughly $100 billion of global stocks to sell. Prime brokerage data show AI net exposure as a share of global net exposure at its lowest since September 2025, while Vincent Lin notes last week saw the third-largest weekly increase in hedge fund ETF shorts in a decade. Cosimo Codacci adds that the S&P forward P/E has de-rated 25% this year to 16x even as Q3 EPS grew more than 30%, but cautions positioning is cleaner rather than washed out, with $150 billion of US equity fund inflows in a month, and that it is too early for a Fed pivot with financial conditions about 95bps tighter than the early-September low. Bobby Molavi notes the B-vs-CCC spread hit 8%, something that has happened fewer than five times since 1996, each time with the S&P falling at least 11.5% from its high (this time: 10.7%).

With Silicon Valley and the rest of the US on holiday yesterday, markets have been experiencing a quiet 24 hours. Without the US in it's difficult to take too many conclusions from the price action but there have been some signs that the tech selloff has stabilised for now, and that risk appetite is returning to markets. We’ve had a decent equity rally, with a sharp rebound in tech stocks pushing Europe’s STOXX 600 (+1.75%) to a one-week high and S&P 500 (+1.79%) and Nasdaq (+2.75%) futures rallying this morning with the former only up around +0.5% for most of yesterday’s European session, so the rally has accelerated overnight. Indeed the KOSPI (+4.81%) is continuing its wild ride with the Nikkei (+1.99%) also posting strong gains and 10yr US Treasuries are +6.4bps to just below 4.92%.

Even as I type Chinese equities are suddenly seeing a big pop higher after the State Council signalled renewed support for the market, including a bigger stabilising role for state-backed funds, measures to draw more long-term capital into equities, and encouragement for companies to increase dividends and buybacks. The Shanghai Composite is +2.95%, rising more than 2.5% since the announcement, while the tech-heavy Star 50 has jumped around 11%. This is also helping the Hang Seng (+2.17%).

Meanwhile, data released earlier this morning showed Tokyo’s core inflation accelerated to 2.9% year-on-year in November from 2.6% in October, marking its fastest pace in 16 months. That was inline with expectations, but headline inflation was three tenths below expectations at 2.8% and core-core two tenths below at 2.5%.

This all follows a good session in Europe yesterday with the risk-on tone clearly back. In fairness, much of that was a catch-up to the US recovery late in the previous session. But the rally gained steam in the afternoon, and the STOXX 600 (+1.75%) closed at a one-week high. Moreover, tech was the strongest sector in the index, and the strongest industry group within that were semiconductors & semiconductor equipment. So it was clear that the most AI-exposed assets were outperforming, and the financial stress was easing on multiple fronts.

That backdrop meant European bond yields moved higher, particularly at the front end as investors priced more hikes from the ECB. In part, that followed the latest ECB minutes, which had several hawkish undertones. For instance, they said that a “large number of members” could have supported an October hike, and it commented that “further tightening was likely necessary”. So alongside the recovery in AI stocks, that meant investors priced in more ECB rate hikes for the months ahead, with 2yr yields in Germany (+3.3bps), France (+0.8bps) and Italy (+1.3bps) all moving higher. Then further out the curve, the 10yr bund yield was only up +2.3bps, whilst 10yr OAT (-1.3bps) and BTP yields (-2.6bps) actually fell, consistent with the wider risk-on move. So that left the Franco-German 10yr spread (-3.6bps) at its tightest in two weeks, at 148bps.

Whilst all that was happening, it’s worth highlighting a new piece here from Mark Wall and Michael Kirker on the major overhaul coming to the ECB’s leadership in 2027. Pablo Hernández de Cos, Markus Brunnermeier and Laurence Boone have been nominated to replace Christine Lagarde, Philip Lane and Isabel Schnabel in the key President, Chief Economist and Head of Markets roles. The team sees the new trio as slightly more dovish overall, but stresses that continuity rather than regime change is the main message. Indeed, Hernández de Cos could conceivably be hiking at his very first meeting as President in March. Our economists' baseline has a final ECB hike to 2.75% in December, but the risk of another move to 3.00% in March is rising. The report also looks at how the new leadership might approach AI, fiscal risks, QT and the TPI, particularly with France potentially testing the ECB’s anti-fragmentation framework. So an interesting set up for 2027. Staying with Europe, remember that Sunday brings the Spanish general election and kick starts a long run of European polls over the next 12 months.

Finally, there were some interesting stories in the commodity space yesterday. That included a fresh rise in oil prices, with Brent crude (+2.07%) rising to $96.57bbl amidst ongoing attacks in the Middle East this week, its highest in almost three weeks. We're up another half a percent this morning.

Looking at the day ahead now, data releases include the November flash CPI prints from France and Spain, along with German unemployment for November, and the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey for October. Otherwise from central banks, we’ll hear from the ECB’s Lane, Nagel, Vujcic and Moulin.

items.title: Black Friday Meets The K-Shaped Economy: Here's What To Expect
items.content_text:
Black Friday Meets The K-Shaped Economy: Here's What To Expect

Nvidia was this week's big market catalyst following Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO. Welcome back. Now, shifting gears, consumers will take center stage with Black Friday at the end of the week and Cyber Monday early next week.

Amazon has already rolled out sales across its electronic device lineup, while Best Buy is promoting doorbuster deals, including 50% off select flat-panel TVs.

The National Retail Federation and Prosper Insights & Analytics published a new report that expects 182.7 million consumers will shop this Thanksgiving weekend, down about 2% from a year earlier.

NRF says the decline is partly because consumers are shopping earlier. About 60% had already begun their holiday shopping at the start of November, up from 56% before the COVID-19 era.

Still, Black Friday remains the most popular shopping day over Thanksgiving weekend, with 69% of prospective shoppers expecting to make purchases that day, followed by Cyber Monday at around 36%, according to NRF's survey of 8,000 consumers.

Adding more color to the holiday spending outlook, Goldman Sachs retail analyst Brooke Roach and her team, including Kate McShane and Eric Sheridan, surveyed roughly 1,000 consumers and found a not-so-surprising widening divide: higher-income households are planning to boost spending, while nearly half of lower-income shoppers expect to cut back.

Half of households earning $100,000 or more plan to spend more this holiday season, up from 44% last year. Among households earning less than $50,000, 48% expect to spend less, up from 46%.

"Optimism remains concentrated among the higher-income consumer while low- and middle-income households remain relatively more cautious," the analysts wrote in a note published Monday.

Here are their key findings:

Planned holiday spending increasingly bifurcated: Overall spend intent modestly improved Y/Y, with fewer consumers planning to spend less on holiday purchases vs. last year. However, spending plans remain bifurcated, with higher-income consumers more likely to plan increased spending this year (50% vs. 44% last year), while low-income consumers remain more cautious, with 48% planning to spend less (vs. 46% last year). 

Planned spend also improved for younger consumers, with Millennials and Gen Z indicating less cautious spending plans vs. last year.

Price inflation still evident but relatively more benign for middle- and high-income consumers: The vast majority of respondents continue to believe gift prices are more expensive this year. However, price perception relatively improved Y/Y amongst middle and high income consumers while perception continued to deteriorate for low-income consumers. Sales and discounts also remain important to respondents' shopping plans, though this trend is largely stable with prior year levels.

Preferred shopping destinations: Amazon and Walmart remain top destinations for holiday shopping. By retailer, Amazon remains firmly in the lead as the top holiday gifting destination, gaining modest share this year (+1pt). Walmart retained its number 2 spot and saw the largest Y/Y increase in share (+7pts).

Category dynamics: Gift cards remain the top gifting choice despite a Y/Y decline. Apparel, toys/games, accessories, and jewelry gained gifting share, while footwear, housewares, media, and experiential gifts softened. In apparel, athletic footwear, athletic apparel, and denim lead in plans to spend more, while dresses, handbags/accessories, and workwear/formal clothing remain the most frequently cited categories for spending cuts.

AI utilization is growing: Around 58% of consumers expect to use AI tools to find, evaluate, or purchase gifts this holiday season (+7pts Y/Y), with 32% indicating increased usage Y/Y (+6pts Y/Y). Younger consumers and men continue to be the most likely to report AI utilization in their gift-giving process.

The analysts nevertheless see a healthy holiday spending backdrop, favoring retailers offering strong deals such as Walmart, Amazon, Urban Outfitters and Aritzia. 

One source of relief for consumers has emerged at the pump: The national average for regular gasoline has fallen to around $3.67 a gallon on Monday morning, down from roughly $4.50 in late September, freeing up some discretionary spending among working poor households. 

The big question heading into Black Friday is whether those savings end up as gifts under the Christmas tree or go toward groceries and utility bills.
