Property taxes are comparatively high in Texas, which has no income tax. “There’s potential common ground emerging between Democrats and Republicans,” Fechter writes. “Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has argued for ending at least some property taxes for homeowners—an idea long sought by conservative lawmakers but largely dismissed given its high cost.” Lawmakers on both sides might be willing to balance that out by “eliminating property and sales tax breaks for corporations, particularly data centers.” But there are a lot of details to hash out, including how to provide similar affordability relief to renters. Read Fechter’s full report for more details.

Elsewhere:

  • Former Georgia House Minority Leader Stacey Abrams argues in The Guardian that democracy advocates need to turn their attention to statewide battles—and quickly. “Where pro-democracy leaders now hold power, they have two jobs. The first is to deliver tangible results, or people will stop showing up. Again,” she writes. “The second is harder: building safeguards that outlast whoever holds office. That means state voting rights laws, fair maps drawn under rules that bind the next majority too, and independent courts that protect criticism of the people in charge. A commitment to democracy includes accepting limits on your own excesses.”
  • Just in time for Thanksgiving, Cami Koons reports for the Iowa Capital Dispatch that the state is almost through with its corn harvest, following delays due to unusually wet weather. Harvests fell behind their usual pace this fall because of an “incredibly rainy” September.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

Public Citizen has identified three Polymarket accounts that placed large winning bets on Nvidia’s leadership drama shortly before Jensen Huang’s return was announced—reportedly at the Trump administration’s explicit request. One of them “sat idle for almost a year, then bought ‘No Change,’ meaning a successor to Huang would not be announced by the end of the year, three times between Nov 17 and Sunday at 1:29 p.m. ET, about $18.2K in all,” for a $128,300 payout. Another “mostly places bets on the Iran war. It put $480 on ‘rejoin by Nov 30’ Sunday at 3:41 p.m. ET, then about $20.2K on ‘No Change’ Monday at 6:38 a.m. and about $8.3K on ‘rejoin by Dec 31’ at 6:40 a.m. Those bets totaling roughly $29,000 yielded a total payout of about $200,000.” On Tuesday, the watchdog called for all the accounts they identified, along with 21 “trades of $3,000 or more” on Kalshi, to be investigated.

On Wednesday at 6 p.m. ET, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace will host an event (online for U.S. participants) called “Can the EU hold its ground?” It will look at Europe’s future in an era where it increasingly seems caught between the U.S., Russia, China, and Turkey. Dimitar Bechev, Tony Barber, and Rosa Balfour will discuss.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Political Trivia Question of the Day  

The last Democratic Senate leadership fight happened in 1994 and came down to one vote. Can you name the two senators involved? One, obviously, was the winner, who would go on to lead the party in the Senate for a decade. The other represented the same state his father had in the Senate.  (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: Trump Wrecks His Own Claims About Jensen Huang With Pardon Offer
items.content_text:
Moneymakers and stars never face their comeuppance in Donald Trump’s world, because, as the president explained in a 2005 hot-mic moment, “when you’re a star … you can do anything.”

The president has offered to pardon newly returned Nvidia chief Jensen Huang—even though he previously insisted Huang had done nothing wrong to prompt his initial ouster from the company.

Trump told the New York Post on Tuesday that a pardon is “always an option.”

Huang resumed his roles as Nvidia’s president, chief executive officer, and member of the board on Monday. The reappointment came mere days after Huang had been tossed out of the company that he co-founded over revelations of his numerous extramarital affairs, the most dubious of which involved a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies identified as a spy and a state asset. The paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation of Jensen’s), had reportedly been in contact with an officer from China’s Ministry of State Security throughout her affair with the Nvidia chief.

Huang is scheduled to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Tuesday and then the Senate Banking Committee two days later to discuss the matter. In his interview with the Post, Trump said he didn’t believe Huang would need to invoke the Fifth Amendment to avoid incriminating himself in the upcoming congressional hearings.

“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump told the Post. “I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100 percent aboveboard, and you know, a very smart person.”

Earlier this week, the president revealed that he personally vouched to Nvidia’s board that Huang was not a national security threat.

Nvidia shares spiraled in the weeks after Huang was ousted from the company, rattling the U.S. economy and Trump’s personal stock portfolio with it: The president’s 2026 financial disclosures revealed that he purchased between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock earlier this year. As of September 30, Trump was believed to have 370,000 shares in Nvidia, according to a review by the Financial Times. Huang’s unexpected reappointment sent the company’s stock skyrocketing, jumping by 31.5 percent and adding some $950 billion to the company’s overall value. Trump, for his part, made up to $15 million, the Financial Times reported.

items.title: Markwayne Mullin’s Job Is In Danger
items.content_text:
Markwayne Mullin is losing the White House.

New reporting from The Washington Post contends that President Trump’s second homeland security secretary is seen as a “liability” by high-ranking officials in the Trump administration, particularly after his awkward, non-reassuring handling of the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide grounding of flights earlier this month—baselessly suggesting that AI might have downed the flights, and taking his own flight to a college football game while every other passenger in the U.S. was stranded.

Mullin was specifically pulled from TV appearances on the issue by newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. The Post also reported that Mullin’s accent and demeanor suggested to those around him that he was not as learned on the issues as he needed to be, and that his closest staffers weren’t, either.

The critics aren’t just in the White House. Conservative commentator Megyn Kelly said on her radio show last week that Mullin seemed “like an idiot.”

“I have zero faith in this man. Zero. Less than zero. And this is a very serious agency, one in which I would like to have some faith in the person heading it up,” Kelly said. Newsmax’s Greg Kelly also referred to Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy as “two bumbling, mumbling, stumbling people.”

Mark Krikorian, executive director at the conservative Center for Immigration Studies, doesn’t think Mullin was ever cut out for the Department of Homeland Security position.

“He was nominated basically to get confirmed quickly,” Krikorian told the Post. “He was in the Senate, people liked him and he got along—so if you pick somebody with that kind of objective, you can’t be surprised if there will be problems.”

Whether it’s Kristi Noem, Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Pam Bondi, Alina Habba, or Katie Zacharia, the Trump administration seems to have a real problem picking individuals who can actually perform. And while this report suggests that Mullin’s days in the administration may be numbered, Trump is standing by him—at least publicly.

“He’s doing a good job. You know, it’s a very thankless job because if you take people out of the country, if you take 100 killers out and you have one person that shouldn’t be on the list, you just get decimated,” the president told the New York Post in an interview published Monday. “So it’s a very tough job.”

items.title: The Infamous DOJ “Slush Fund” Is Back—and Just as Corrupt as Before
items.content_text:
Remember how the administration killed Donald Trump’s $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization” slush fund in August under a barrage of bipartisan outrage? It turns out that the same month, the Justice Department quietly resurrected the same lawless strategy in a lawsuit over the very same IRS leak.

A recent report in ProPublica laid bare the intervention of top Trump appointees at the DOJ to pay outsize sums to friends of Donald. The beneficiaries here are not, to be sure, January 6 insurrectionists. Rather, they include a golf pro at one of Trump’s clubs and two other Trump employees. After career lawyers had contested the claims for more than a year, DOJ political operatives swooped in and bestowed $500,000 apiece—500 times the statutory amount—on five plaintiffs.

The slush fund approach is back. It just moved to Maryland.

Trump’s initial lawsuit against the IRS was a $10 billion claim over the leak of his tax returns by a contractor, not an IRS employee, named Charles Littlejohn. The Justice Department colluded with Trump for an outsize award of a $1.776 billion slush fund and amnesty potentially worth $100 million. Judge Kathleen Williams found that the whole thing had been collusive and the lawsuit served as legal cover for a deal with no viable basis in law or fact. That decision remains under appeal in the Eleventh Circuit.

The fund produced a huge controversy that, for a time, impeded Todd Blanche’s confirmation to be attorney general. He offered the Senate Judiciary Committee the empty declaration that “the weaponization fund is dead.” But in the same hearing, he left the door ajar, suggesting the department could essentially do it anyway, with or without a court.

I said at the time that his assertion was dead wrong, and it was. But now the DOJ has adopted it, abandoning its adversary role and showering favored plaintiffs with grossly unwarranted recoveries.

Safe Harbor International LLC v. Booz Allen Hamilton is a consolidated class action by five plaintiffs alleging the precise same behavior and legal violation as in Trump’s case—that Booz Allen, Littlejohn’s employer, showed negligence in allowing Littlejohn to leak income tax records.

The plaintiffs brought the case in January 2025. For more than a year, DOJ’s career lawyers fought it. In March, the Maryland district court judge hearing the case denied the defendants’ motions to dismiss and ordered the DOJ to file an answer to the complaint. A few more months of bona fide litigation followed, taking the case to the eve of discovery.

The case was then suddenly wrenched into reverse when political leadership of the DOJ stepped in in August—the same month Blanche formally rescinded Trump’s fund. Brett Shumate, the head of the Civil Division, and Joshua Wu, a deputy assistant attorney general, seized responsibility for the case from the career attorney who had been defending it. They stopped the defense and ordered up a unilateral proposal to the five named plaintiffs, styled as an offer of judgment: $500,000 apiece, or $2.5 million in all.

Shumate and Wu signed the offer sheet; the career trial attorney handling the case, who would ordinarily sign it, did not. Nobody consulted the IRS Office of Chief Counsel, as is standard practice. IRS employees nevertheless objected that the offer far exceeded what the law called for and that no evidence supported it.

Even the feature Trump touted as the beneficent heart of his deal—a fund to compensate third parties who supposedly had been mistreated by the government—shows up here. Only now the third parties are his friends. The golf pro is Shelby Lowman, whose paintings of the course Trump has autographed for club prizes. Safe Harbor is an obscure Delaware LLC with no public presence, whose investors include a trading executive whose firm put $100 million into Trump Media after the Securities and Exchange Commission dropped a case against his crypto company.

After the $2.5 million deal was struck, two more people turned up seeking to keep the case going: a retired accountant at the same Trump club and, apparently, a former lifeguard at another Trump course. The plaintiffs claim that their class consists of tens or hundreds of thousands of people. At $500,000 a head, you can do the math.

It was only the diligent reporting by ProPublica that turned up the $2.5 million deal. DOJ did nothing to publicize it. And for all we know, there are more.

The core illegality and abuse of executive power are the same issues that Judge Williams had identified in the Trump case. This is not a bona fide settlement. It’s a payout to friends engineered by a supine DOJ that decided for political reasons to roll over and play dead.

We know that’s so for two reasons. First, the statute provides $1,000 for each unauthorized disclosure; anything more requires proof of actual damages, and these plaintiffs hadn’t offered any. Rather than fight, DOJ folded and offered 500 times the statutory figure, before any final decision and at the cost of any right to appeal. A former head of the Tax Division’s appellate section told ProPublica the deal is “not passing the smell test.”

Second, the case lacks merit. The statute lets taxpayers sue the United States for disclosures by officers and employees of the government. But Littlejohn was only a contractor. Rather than press that defense at summary judgment or on appeal, the DOJ simply dropped it.

The White House says the DOJ is “promoting efficient resolution of cases to avoid ‘extraordinary liability.’” But there’s no extraordinary liability in play. Based on other similar cases, the administration’s total liability is zero. The extraordinary liability is rather the dispensation of millions of dollars in public money to friendly plaintiffs.

Most importantly, the department seeks to pay these plaintiffs from the Judgment Fund, which Congress set up for the DOJ to fund bona fide settlements against the United States: real claims, actually contested, that the government resolves to serve the public interest. It is not a private piggy bank for Trump to draw on to advance his political purposes.

The White House and DOJ apparently were banking on keeping the raw payout under the radar. That’s going to be a lot harder now that a new set of sheriffs is coming to town on Capitol Hill.

The Safe Harbor deal should be the subject of hearings to determine just what happened. If the administration insists the deal is legit, it should let its officials come forward and explain how paying a Trump golf pro half a million dollars serves a public purpose. And then there are the other beneficiaries of the $500,000 each. If Congress starts asking them questions, they can’t hide behind claims of executive privilege.

Congress can do more than ask. Acting as a body, the new Democratic House can drive home that the Judgment Fund by its terms can be used only for bona fide settlements, not collusive arrangements such as this and the Trump case. It also may be able to sue in the institution’s own name to obtain a declaratory judgment that the fund may not be used to pay for collusive cases.

Happy Thanksgiving to the golf pro. Looks like the rest of us are picking up the check.

items.title: Transcript: Trump Nvidia Mess Worsens as Todd Blanche Presser Implodes
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 25 episode of The Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

Donald Trump’s Nvidia scandal just took another ugly turn. Now that Trump got Nvidia to rehire its leader, Jensen Huang, claiming his affair with a potential Chinese honeypot isn’t that big a deal, reporters sharply questioned Attorney General Todd Blanche about this whole fiasco. It didn’t go well. Blanche refused to say whether Huang has been investigated at all, and refused to clarify why Trump is claiming he’s been exonerated. This means the whole scandal now involves how federal law enforcement is handling the situation as well.

So we’re talking to Jamie Raskin, the next chair of the Judiciary Committee, about how Democrats will scrutinize this part of the story in the new Congress, and what that should ideally look like. Congressman, thanks so much for joining us.

Jamie Raskin: I’m psyched to be with you, Greg.

Sargent: So Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate its leader, Jensen Huang, even though U.S. intelligence suspected he had an affair with Alice Huang, no relation, who was allegedly passing advanced AI technology to China.

Trump claimed a very thorough investigation found nothing amiss and relayed this to Nvidia’s board. Congressman, before we get to whether there was an investigation, what’s your 30,000-foot view of this whole scandal? How bad is it?

Raskin: It’s terrible. We have to determine what Secretary of Commerce Lutnick was doing and who he was representing. Was it the interests of his family firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, and his sons and himself financially? Or was it the interests of these other companies around the world who are trafficking the AI chips and computers to China? Was it the interest of the Chinese government?

It certainly was not the American people. So we really have to identify precisely who he was acting for. And I assume that he’s in alignment with Donald Trump on it. Both of them, personally, were making a lot of money on Nvidia and had a lot of Nvidia stock.

Sargent: Right. So Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was someone who just really kind of let us all down by not getting on top of the situation, even as he appears to have been making money off of it, right?

Raskin: That’s right. Look, we have laws for a reason. So we had export restrictions on people moving AI chips and computers to China, on the theory that we are in this rivalry, or AI arms race, with China. So he circumvented it, and he moved to weaken the export laws.

That apparently is not in the interests of America, at least as they’re telling it, because they’re keeping the American people and Congress and the states away from doing any regulation of artificial intelligence, whether we’re talking about data centers or labor and environmental questions, or just national security and human security.

So they’ve kept the people away, but then Donald Trump goes over and he’s yucking it up with the prime minister of China, with Xi, the head of the Chinese Communist Party, and Vladimir Putin. It looks like a triumvirate of autocrats from around the world making their own decisions, making money off of the rest of us, and reducing American national security to an afterthought.

Donald Trump has already said, No, he doesn’t think about inflation and the cost to the American people. And evidently they don’t think about national security either.

Sargent: It’s in this context that Attorney General Todd Blanche talked to reporters on Tuesday. One of these reporters pointed out that Trump had said Jensen Huang had been exonerated. The reporter then asked Blanche, well, did Trump’s conclusion come after any kind of investigation into Huang’s conduct? First you hear the reporter, then you hear Blanche. Listen.

Reporter (voiceover): Did the Justice Department investigate Jensen, or was that conclusion reached without an investigation?

Todd Blanche (voiceover): Well, so, no, what the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him. And so I’m not going to get into communications I had with the president about it, but you shouldn’t—what he was saying was true, right? So what he was saying is exactly right, which is that to the extent that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true.


Sargent: Congressman, Blanche doesn’t say one way or the other if Huang faced any kind of investigation. Is that good enough? And what’s your response?

Raskin: Well, that was extremely evasive and slippery, even by Todd Blanche standards. He seems to acknowledge at the end that there was no investigation. But Donald Trump sees exoneration wherever he wants to see exoneration. He declared himself exonerated by the Epstein files, when they haven’t released millions of documents.

And still, it’s very clear he’s indicted by the Epstein files. We did a complete report on how there was clearly enough evidence to pursue a real investigation just based on the mentions of Donald Trump that they allowed us to see.

So this strikes me as exactly parallel to that. They think that Mr. Huang has been exonerated by an investigation that never took place.

Sargent: Right. It may or may not have. Anyway, Trump did say DOJ exonerated Huang, and that this was a reason he pressured Nvidia’s board to rehire him. Now, Blanche himself had previously said the FBI was looking into the allegations about Huang and his affair.

Blanche was pressed on this, too, on Tuesday, and he refused to say what it meant. FBI Director Kash Patel refused to say whether the FBI had interviewed Huang. Congressman, where are we? What do we know about whether law enforcement looked at the situation or not?

Raskin: Todd Blanche has been perfectly clear that he’s the lawyer only to Donald Trump. He was his personal attorney. He became his personal attorney general. I can’t imagine that they would have engaged in a real, meaningful investigation of Huang.

I tend to doubt that they would have even done a perfunctory and formalistic one. But if there is one, they should tell us exactly why the president is running around saying that Huang has been somehow exonerated.

He’s exonerated only because their finances are implicated by Nvidia and by all of the AI money. They’re not thinking about the economic security of America, and they’re not thinking about the national security of Americans.

They’re thinking about their cabal of the president and his family and the Cabinet officers and their family and whatever tiny group of people they think they represent.

Sargent: Well, is one of the outstanding questions here whether Trump ordered an end to an investigation into Huang? Because, again, Blanche seemed to suggest at some point that something was being looked at, in his words. So don’t we need to know whether Trump essentially said, Hey, Todd, put an end to this?

Raskin: We need to know whether there was an investigation or there was not. And if there was, what were the actual results of it? What were the conclusions? What was the evidence it’s based on? And if it was terminated, why was it terminated? And why did the president say that Huang was exonerated by it?

But until we have some actual facts there, all that we can conclude is that Trump declared him exonerated because Trump wanted him exonerated, in the same way that Trump wanted to be exonerated by the Epstein files. But he was anything but that.

Sargent: Well, at this point, this whole scandal now clearly encapsulates federal law enforcement as well. And obviously the House Judiciary Committee, which you’ll be chairing, has a big oversight role over DOJ.

In the context of everything we heard from Blanche and Patel there, what will the Judiciary Committee seek to determine about law enforcement’s conduct on all this? What will you look into?

Raskin: Well, we want those basic facts. We would like to know whether there was an investigation or not. But more profoundly, we need to know who exactly Howard Lutnick was acting on behalf of in this whole sequence of events. He was supposed to be enforcing the export laws of the United States, not circumnavigating them, not undermining them, and not weakening them.

The sugar-high bounce in the stock market has already come back down. So even the only people that they care about, which is people who own stock in Nvidia, even they are really going to be taking a second look at this whole thing.

Should we have the president of the United States dictating to a private corporation who their CEO is, based on recent meetings with the prime minister of China? And should we have a private corporation dictating the foreign policy and the trade policy of the United States?

This feels a lot more like a MAGA corporate state than it does either a representative constitutional democracy or a free market. It’s beginning to operate a lot more like a Russian corporate autocracy, with Vladimir Putin and his oligarchs, or like the Stalinist state apparatus of China. But it doesn’t resemble the way that the American government should be working, or even the way that it has worked in the past.

Sargent: For this to all be unfolding, you’d need DOJ and FBI to essentially be taking a step back and taking a hands-off approach, simply because Trump has declared that Jensen Huang is his guy. So I just want to confirm that the Judiciary Committee will look at, will probe, will investigate what DOJ and FBI are doing here. Can you confirm that for us?

Raskin: Well, if I’ve got anything to do with it, Greg. I should say, though, that, you know, this crisis and this scandal is popping out, like, on a daily basis now. We’ve not been together since these recent events.

And so, we have a number of committees that have an interest in it, and so we’re going to have to sort out all of those territorial issues. But like I always say, there’s enough corruption in Trumpland to go around. So I can guarantee that there will be a bunch of committees seeking to look into this.

Sargent: Right. So whoever it is, House Democrats in one committee or another will examine how DOJ is handling this piece of the whole scandal.

Raskin: Well, it is both a central crisis in the real world and an emblematic crisis of the way things have come to work. We have corporate interests dictating national security, economic, and trade policy, and then we’ve got the president of the United States acting like Mussolini, trying to determine the actions of private corporations and dictating to them who their leader is going to be. It’s an extraordinary situation.

Sargent: And possibly telling DOJ and FBI not to investigate something with very clear national security implications, right?

Raskin: Absolutely, because they’ve destroyed even the traditional and normative division between the political interests or financial interests of the president and the independence of the law enforcement function. That’s gone.

So it goes without saying that if Donald Trump wants something done, this Department of Injustice, as we call it, will follow in his wake and do whatever he wants him to do.

That’s why we saw so much hemming and hawing and evasiveness by the attorney general when he was questioned by a reporter about this. He basically didn’t want to contradict the president, but I think he knew that there was not a real, authentic investigation. Or if there was, or if it started out that way, it was terminated for political reasons.

Sargent: Right. So if that could have happened, then, whichever committee we’re talking about here, it would presumably entail bringing in Blanche and Patel, or trying to, and subpoenaing them if necessary, to get them under oath to talk about what happened here.

And it would presumably entail a demand for communications between Trump, the White House, and these DOJ officials about the whole Huang scandal, right?

Raskin: That would be the logical implication, yes.

Sargent: Well, so assuming that when you investigate this, Trump and Blanche claim executive privilege to shield communications about this from Congress, what happens then? I think you and I talked about this in another context.

Should Democrats be ready to use the power of the purse to compel DOJ and other agencies beyond this one to comply with legitimate oversight demands? What’s that going to look like? You and I talked about it, but I’d like to hear it again.

Raskin: The power of the purse is central here, because the Constitution is designed in such a way that it is only Congress that controls the purse strings for government. And, you know, certain kinds of bills have to originate in the House of Representatives, but it’s the House and the Senate together that decide on monetary matters.

And so we’re not going to allow a situation to proceed in which the money of the people is being used for purposes that are unlawful and contrary to the Constitution. That’s just not going to happen. So we’re going to be very serious about the appropriations power.

And we’re not limited to the appropriations power. Obviously we have the very comprehensive investigative oversight powers when it comes to the execution of our policymaking functions. And where there are legislative purposes that we have, the Supreme Court has been perfectly clear that we have a right to get all of the information that we need.

Sargent: Well, Republicans and MAGA figures are also turning on the administration. Congressman Pat Harrigan said Huang’s reinstatement means, “one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of adherence to the rule of law.” That was a Republican talking.

Republican Senator Rick Scott, who’s also MAGA, said this whole mess, “looks terrible on its face,” adding, “The federal government owes the American people answers about what actually happened.” Senator Tom Cotton said, “I think we need to catalog the damage that’s been done.”

Congressman, is there any basis for a real bipartisan investigation, and possibly policy response, to this whole situation once Dems take over? Is that at all plausible?

Raskin: Well, I certainly hope so. Republicans in the past have made certain noises about public integrity when it comes to Trump, and they end up chickening out in the end and prove themselves to be servile and invertebrate agents of Trump.

But if they want to participate with us, we would love to have them do it. We have something approaching a two-to-one majority in the House of Representatives, and a big majority in the Senate too.

So we’re not going to wait on them. But if they want to come forward and, at this point, begin to extricate themselves from the avalanche of corruption and pay-to-play government that Trump has given us, that’s all to the good. Maybe they’ll be able to rescue their party. But in any event, we’re not waiting around for them.

Sargent: Right. There are just parts of the MAGA coalition which seem to be somewhat genuinely hawkish about China. You’d think that you’d be able to get those types of people involved in something like this, wouldn’t you?

Raskin: Yeah. The truth is that Donald Trump has dozens of times praised President Xi. He calls him an outstanding, amazing leader, right out of central casting: He’s got the brains, he’s got the looks, he controls 1.4 billion people with an iron fist. Trump marvels at the powers and the authoritarian levers that Xi has and that Vladimir Putin has. He emulates those people. He wants to be those people.

Never does Trump have a word for the Uyghurs. Never does he have a word for the Tibetans, people in Taiwan, people in Hong Kong, not at all. He never says a word for Russian dissidents or human rights activists. These are really his people.

So to the extent that the Republicans want to join us in a campaign for human rights and democracy around the world, great. But right now, it’s very clear that Trump and the Republican Party have been on the firm side of the autocrats.

Sargent: Final question. Could you just talk a little more about what it means that DOJ, the Department of Justice, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation appear to be now part of this?

It seems pretty critical, because what you’d need for all this stuff to unfold kind of under cover of darkness is for people like Todd Blanche and Kash Patel to be pliably agreeing to Trump’s command that they step back from all this stuff and just—speaking constitutionally, that seems bad, Congressman.

Raskin: Well, we’ve been here before. The Department of Justice has been in the lead of the cover-up of the Epstein files. They’ve done everything in their power to sweep it under the rug, to deny that there is sufficient evidence even to have an investigation.

We’re talking about a billion-dollar multinational global sex-trafficking conspiracy, and they say there’s nothing in any of those documents that would lead them to have an investigation. And so they’ve tried to bury the whole thing, because obviously Donald Trump wants the whole thing to go away.

But it’s the same thing with the corruption of the government contracting system. It’s the same thing with Donald Trump Jr.’s manipulation of his insider knowledge in order to make 2,000 percent returns on his private investment firm, 1789. The Department of Justice is nowhere to be found on any of those things.

He really is acting just like Donald Trump’s attorney. We basically have this huge private law firm just to work for Donald Trump, in the interests of him and his family. And you see it with the pardons, everywhere you turn.

And so for many Americans who are just tuning in to this side of it, yes, they will be scandalized to see that the attorney general is acting in this way, but he’s very forthright about it.

Sargent: Right. And it couldn’t be happening, is what I want to try to get at—you couldn’t have this scandal unfolding if you had a DOJ and FBI actually investigating what happened with the Huang affair.

Raskin: Right. Congress has to fill in, because we don’t have a Department of Justice with any concept of the rule of law and constitutional government. They believe that we live in some kind of monarchical fiefdom, where everybody in their branch just serves the interests of Donald Trump and his family.

It’s just an outrageous turn of events in the 21st century. But they want America to become like the autocratic governments that they’re in league with, like in Russia and China, and, hey, North Korea. I mean, Kim Jong Un—Donald Trump loves him too. He marvels at his form of government.

So our job is to reassert the powers of Congress now, the lawmaking branch, which Madison called the preeminent branch of government in the Federalist Papers, in order to pursue popular objectives, democratic goals, and to restore constitutional government to our people.

Sargent: Congressman Jamie Raskin, you’re certainly going to have your work cut out for you. Thanks for coming on with us, as always.

Raskin: You bet, Greg.

items.title: Congratulations, North Carolina. You Finally Got Rid of Virginia Foxx.
items.content_text:
It’s bad form to gloat over the misfortune of others, but I think we can make an exception for Representative Virginia Foxx.

When Chuck Hubbard was declared victor Sunday in North Carolina’s 5th congressional district, Democrats acquired their largest House majority in this (admittedly still young) century. That’s cause for celebration. But that Hubbard beat out the 11-term Foxx is cause for even greater celebration. She’s as nasty a piece of work as you’ll encounter in Washington.

Gloating can be risky. The Republicans could stage a comeback in two years’ time. It’s pretty hard to imagine right now, but last time the Democrats won 258 House seats was 1992, and in the very next election Republicans won their first House majority in four decades. Still, gloating over Foxx’s demise is pretty safe. At 83, she is in no position to mount a comeback. Her political career is over. Rejoice.

Foxx is probably labor’s single biggest enemy in Congress. She doesn’t hold the absolute lowest lifetime ranking on the AFL-CIO’s legislative scorecard, but as a two-time chair of the House Education and Labor Committee (whose name the GOP always changes when it comes to power to “Education and the Workforce” because the word labor gives Republicans the fantods), she is certainly the most viciously anti-union. Other Republicans may vote against labor, but only Foxx posted on her congressional website a Reuters hit piece quoting her saying organized labor “lost its reason for being” because Congress passed too many laws protecting workers.

Foxx puts her money where her mouth is, even when it means certain defeat. In 2021, Foxx led Republican opposition to the Protecting the Right to Organize Act, or PRO, a vitally important labor bill repealing much of 1947’s anti-labor Taft-Hartley Act, which proceeded over the next four decades to bleed unions dry. The PRO Act passed anyway, picking up five Republican votes before dying in the Senate. During Covid, Foxx wrote labor leaders to demand that union dues be suspended. The labor leaders ignored her. In the Biden years, Foxx opposed a proposed “walkaround” rule allowing union representatives to attend workplace safety inspections at nonunion sites. The walkaround rule took effect in spite of her objections.

In 2025, Foxx became chair of the powerful House Rules Committee, where she blocked a Democratic amendment to release the Epstein files (later achieved through discharge petition) and pushed through a resolution barring the House from voting on a Senate resolution of disapproval against Trump’s tariffs (later overturned by the Supreme Court). Foxx got the same resolution through the Rules Committee in 2026, but that time the prohibition failed on the House floor.

Foxx doesn’t confine her toxicity to condemning labor unions as cesspools of corruption “bought and paid for” by Democrats. She also terrorizes young people and their loved ones. Last spring, Foxx wrote a 10-year-old constituent that his teacher “will not be able to give you a good educational experience.… Because they are too interested in indoctrinating you.” In a House floor speech attended by the mother of Matthew Shepard, Foxx said it was “a hoax” that Shepard’s killers, one of whom admitted to being in a state of “gay panic,” committed a hate crime. “It’s an urban myth,” Foxx said. “And I’d tell her that man did land on the moon and the moon wasn’t made out of green cheese.” Foxx later said that “the term ‘hoax’ was a poor choice of words.” 

Foxx was one of the 129 House Republicans (plus eight senators) who voted against certifying Joe Biden as the winner of the 2020 election. When a reporter asked Mike Johnson, then a nominee for House speaker, about his efforts to overturn the 2020 election, Foxx said, “Shut up.”

Foxx began her career in higher education, an unusual pedigree for a MAGA hack. She taught English at a community college and then sociology at Appalachian State University. (Foxx holds a master’s degree in sociology, but her doctorate is in education.) At Appalachian State, Foxx rose to assistant dean before assuming the presidency of Mayland Community College in Spruce Pine, North Carolina. Despite her background teaching and administering at colleges and universities, Foxx is today almost pathologically opposed to student debt relief.  

“I have very little tolerance for people who tell me that they graduate with $200,000 of debt or even $80,0000 of debt because there’s no reason for that,” Foxx said during a 2012 appearance on the radio show of Watergate felon G. Gordon Liddy.

In 1994, Foxx was elected to the North Carolina state Senate, which became her springboard into Congress. As a state senator, Foxx was reportedly a standard-issue conservative, willing on occasion to work with Democrats. When she arrived in Congress in 2005, Foxx said she didn’t always support Republican positions. But Congress was already getting hyperpartisan and Foxx is a quick study. After Hurricane Katrina, Foxx was one of only two House freshmen and only two House Southerners to oppose disaster aid to Louisiana. 

Foxx can sometimes be capable of breathtaking hypocrisy. In 2021, Salon reported that Foxx’s investment of $79,000 to $210,000 in Altria stock likely made her the House’s biggest investor in marijuana-related stock—even though Foxx voted consistently against marijuana decriminalization. (Atria, better known as a tobacco company, owns about 41 percent of Cronos Group, a leading cannabis company.) “Democrats can’t get their minds off pot bills,” Foxx posted on X in 2020. “No wonder their minority is shrinking.” And also: “What are Republicans fighting to protect? Jobs. What are Democrats fighting to protect? Pot. What a joke.”

This Thanksgiving season, when you fire up a doob and count life’s blessings, don’t forget that Virginia Foxx will no longer haunt the halls of Congress. I certainly won’t.

items.title: This Is Not the Way to Abolish the Electoral College
items.content_text:
The 2026 midterm elections saw Democrats win popular majorities in states long written off as irredeemably red and dark purple. But blue state Democrat legislators could sink this chance to regain lost constituencies and reset the national political map, by enacting a misguided work-around to supplant the state-by-state structure undergirding the Electoral College. If they are not careful, they could turn a blue wave into a dead-end quagmire.  

The proposed scheme is an interstate agreement, technically known as a “compact”—the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, or NPVIC—that its architects claim could “bypass” the constitutionally prescribed Electoral College without taking on the futile odyssey of attempting to amend the Constitution. After the dust had settled on Election Day, Democrats had taken control of state legislatures and governorships in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin, and Nevada. None of these states had previously agreed to the compact. But if all five agree to join, the total number of electoral votes apportioned based on the national popular vote jumps to 283—enough to end the Electoral College tradition.

Since Republican George W. Bush entered the White House in 2000 with a razor-thin majority of electoral votes (271 of the requisite 270), while his opponent, Democrat Al Gore, won the popular vote by a comparably slim margin of 0.52 percent of the more than 101 million votes cast, Democrats and liberals have demonized the Electoral College, characterizing it as uniquely biased against them and inimical to democratic (small-d) governance.

But, as I detailed after Donald Trump narrowly won the 2024 election, this perception is simply dead wrong. The Constitution in no way mandates the state-by-state winner-take-all system that liberals have decried. Rather, the Framers’ terms dictate merely that each state must be allocated electors matching the number of its respective Senate and House seats. But its provisions give each state discretion to decide how to select their electors (consistent with other constitutional provisions, such as the Bill of Rights, Reconstruction, Progressive-era, and kindred twentieth-century amendments). Hence, near-national winner-take-all exists because individual states voluntarily adopted it, having determined that approach boosts their clout with the federal government.

By 1836, all but one state had chosen winner-take-all. By 1880, all states did so. Currently, all 50 states except two, Maine and Nebraska, plus the District of Columbia, embrace it. Further, over the nation’s history, any partisan tilt of the system, to the extent that it has measurably existed, has often shifted, due to demographic, economic, policy, and technological changes—as Democratic strategists expect it will shift their way in 2028.

The concept of an interstate compact to substitute a national majority popular vote approach originated early in the present century, when Democrats’ path to the White House seemed more daunting than it appears today—though even then, events intervened and Democrats won the presidency in the next two cycles and three of the next five. The idea had distinguished parentage; in particular, a 2007 paper by the Yale Law constitutional savant Akhil Amar.

A cadre of enthusiasts took up the idea for such a constitutional work-around, and formed a 501(c)(4) nonprofit organization, National Popular Vote, to draft the NPVIC and promote it in state capitals. In essence, the terms of the measure bind a state to cast all its electoral votes for the presidential candidate who wins a majority of popular votes nationwide, regardless of who wins a majority of that state’s voters.

As of November 2026, 18 states and Washington, D.C., had adopted legislation to join the NPVIC. Together, they represent 222 Electoral College votes—82 percent of the 270 votes needed for the agreement to go into effect. After November 3, liberals trumpeted that, as Mother Jones headlined, “America Finally Has the Votes to End the Electoral College.”

Deploying their newfound power to push the NPVIC across that finish line would constitute a historic, catastrophic mistake, contravening the transformational lessons liberal leaders should have learned (and voters conservative as well as liberal did learn) from the traumatic Trump decade. Significantly, Akhil Amar, whose 2007 paper and drafting expertise provided critical impetus for the compact, has over the intervening years developed reservations about his idea. On November 8, he shared with an MS NOW interviewer what amounted to a repudiation of the NPVIC and the specific provisions of the one now on the cusp of taking effect. To date, that interview has received scant coverage.


Amar’s turnabout acknowledges the lessons that other liberal leaders have missed. The first lesson, of course, the 180-degree shift of the 2026 election itself. In my 2024 critique, I contended that liberals were scapegoating the “Electoral College,” to sidestep their surest and most efficient route to rebalance power over presidential selection. That route was to play the politics right by tailoring candidates and appeals to the flyover states and constituencies that their coastal elites’ inbred parochialism had driven away. Lo and behold, this time around they did just that.

Granted, Democrats’ huge victory could be a one-off aberration. Its trigger was Republicans’ obeisance to an unhinged leader indifferent to popular needs and aspirations. That said, postmortem analyses reveal changes that with responsive politicking can make the electoral map competitive, or even tilt blue. For starters, look at Texas. A November 16 Wall Street Journal account revealed potentially durable reasons why:

Every Texas county swung to the left, some by more than 70 points. Latino voters, who had moved to the right in recent cycles, swung 37 points leftward. White voters with a college degree swung 15 points in that direction; those without a degree moved 13 points; young voters, 54 points; seniors, 12 points; and small towns and rural areas, 22 points.

Hispanics alone comprise 32 percent of Texas’s eligible voters (and 40 percent of all Texas residents). Their shift was prompted not only by inflation, like all voters, but by anger at Republican-supported ICE brutality toward their community, as well as other grievances common to working- and middle-class voters across the board. Texas has 40 electoral votes, second only to California. Surely, Democratic political leaders can find ways to deepen traction with Hispanics and constituencies that flipped in 2026, sufficient to make Texas’s 40 electoral votes at least competitive, if not tilting blue. Democrats would thence start off presidential campaigns with three of the top four states (California, Texas, and New York), totaling 113 votes in their column, plus scores more from other purple and blue states.

The Texas turnaround is part of a broader prospect. On Sunday, November 15, Mississippi Senator-elect Scott Colom told Meet the Press interviewers that Democrats “need to put senators like myself in position where we can deliver for the rural South, where we can be leaders in ways that show the voters in [all of] rural America that we care about them, that we want them to be successful.” (Emphasis mine.)

Further in that vein, as Harold Meyerson detailed in the November 13 American Prospect, “There are deeper reasons why Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina have become politically purple.… All three states are increasingly dominated by metropolitan areas, populated by racially diverse professionals, racially diverse service-sector workers, young newcomers from neighboring states and distant lands.” Understanding these “tectonic shifts,” Meyerson notes, can enable Democrats to “create what might become a new political majority.”

A still broader perspective is warranted. The 2026 blue wave marked a historic triumph for the Civil Rights Movements of the 1960s, ’70s, and ’80s. Red and dark purple jurisdictions flipped not despite Black, brown, and female priorities but because of these formerly embattled minorities’ mobilization—and broadly shared commonsense, center-left concerns, including by white male cohorts.

The second lesson from the Trump-driven turmoil is this: The Framers were correct to delineate not only a federal chief executive powerful enough to lead and defend a far-flung nation but also intricate institutional checks and balances to constrain a demagogic wannabe dictator abusing those vast powers to shred constitutional democracy and the rule of law. In particular, we have seen the indispensable role of federalism—devolution of substantial legal authority and political autonomy to states. Under Trump, a large portion of the pushback successes by liberals and others—against, for example, abusive immigration enforcement, domestic military repression, and federally manipulated elections—have relied on constitutionally prescribed state authority. Junking the Constitution’s state-grounded framework for selecting presidents—which grants the president zero basis for meddling and Congress merely a limited oversight and backup role—would upend those foundational safeguards.

Those two lessons augur against replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote model by any procedure, including a constitutional amendment. But those drawbacks would be exponentially magnified, and others added, by the legally vulnerable NPVIC proposal now before state legislatures.

The NPVIC has advanced rapidly for three reasons. First, stealth—unintentional but de facto: The national media has had little to say about the compact, which has kept the electorate in the dark about the general idea and its disruptive consequences. Second, the stated goals of the compact—national majority rule; one-person, one vote; equal weight for each American’s vote—resonate as unobjectionable and as American as apple pie. That perception, plus the delusion of liberals that the current system structurally disadvantages them, has led politicians to sign on with little thought and no attention to details or the lack thereof, or the real-world fallout.

Those textual and practical infirmities led Akhil Amar to pump the brakes on enacting the compact during a postelection interview with MS NOW’s Jacob Soboroff. Amar explained that while he is “one of the co-inventors” of the NPVIC, he wasn’t “sure that it’s actually in its current incarnation a great idea.” Amar framed his concerns as tentative. In his view, the states should not rush to embrace the compact. Instead, he recommended “going slow” and having a “national conversation” about the issue.

However, his criticisms—which echo points spelled out by other critics—undermine the whole idea of replacing the Electoral College’s state-by-state regime with a national popular vote system. 

Amar pointed out that, if the goal is “one person, one vote,” that cannot be achieved “without a lot of central oversight because different states let people vote in different ways.” As legal scholar David Beier has detailed: “In [three jurisdictions] people with felony convictions never lose the right to vote. Twenty-three [restore it for former prisoners] when people leave prison.” Fifteen do so [only after] parole and probation. Ten disenfranchise prisoners permanently or erect additional hurdles. Beier adds, “Some states let 17-year-olds vote in primaries if they will be 18 by the general election; others do not.”

All states but one (Mississippi) prescribe procedures for recounts, but their terms vary widely. The NPVIC, however, prescribes no provision for postelection dispute resolution. States could let 17- or 16-year-olds vote, or otherwise configure their rules for partisan, or discriminatory, reasons. But under the NPVIC all states would be compelled to accept other states’ certification of their results, with no way of challenging them. The 2000 Florida postelection brouhaha was a walk in the park compared to what such disputes would look like in the NPVIC’s national popular vote system.

The big problem here is that spelling out uniform rules essential for any national election scheme would require a federal statute, flatly barred by the Constitution. For that reason, it would not be possible without a forbiddingly complex statute and/or amendment.

But there’s a more fundamental issue in play. After what the nation has gone through in the past decade, who would want a presidential election system managed by the president? As Amar asked rhetorically, would we want federal monitors picked by this or any president at every polling place purporting to enforce federal election rules? That is, of course, exactly what Trump fought to impose and, thankfully, what the federal courts, including the Supreme Court, have blocked him from doing—on constitutional grounds.

All of these defects puncture the illusion that adopting the NPVIC will immediately enshrine a one-person, one-vote election system. On the contrary, the instant that NPVIC takes effect, multiple well-prepared lawsuits will hit the courts. Such litigation could drag on for months or years, unless it is somehow terminated by the Supreme Court. As suggested by the above-noted particularly glaring glitches, the overwhelming likelihood is that the court will strike it down, quite likely with more than the six conservative justices’ votes.

Numerous plausible constitutional objections have been proffered by a spectrum of experts. The simplest, most likely overruling ground will be the Constitution’s curt specification “that No state shall, without the consent of Congress, enter into any agreement or compact with any other state.” Securing such assent to any radically transformative presidential election scheme, certainly the one currently in play, would be a daunting process, provision for which the crafters of NPVIC conspicuously left out. There is no realistic chance that the courts, certainly the Supreme Court, will overlook that omission.


As I noted in 2024, there is at least one sound, legal, and feasible electoral reform alternative to constitutional amendment or a “bypass” interstate compact bound to fail in court. This approach is expanding the membership of the House of Representatives.

Respecting the preference of a majority of individual voters is, for sure, a fundamental goal of the Constitution’s plan for our democratic republic. But ensuring due regard for regional interests is likewise an appropriate, even essential goal. After the 2016 election, Democrats decried the fact that Hillary Clinton won the national popular vote by (approximately) 2.9 million votes. But outside of California, which she won by approximately 4.2 million votes, Clinton trailed Trump’s popular vote by 1.3 million votes. Giving some weight to intercoastal regions is a legitimate instrument for reinforcing all major constituencies’ stake in nationhood. Some weight—but probably not today’s 700 percent difference between the voting power of individual citizens of, say, Wyoming and California.

That gross discrepancy is due to the fact that a requirement of two Senate seats for each state is embedded in the constitutional formula for allocating electors among states. But that formula specifies that the “number” of each state’s electors must be “equal to the whole Number of Senators and representatives” of each state. Unlike the upper House, the number of representatives requires only legislation to change.

For over a century, since 1910, that number has been fixed at 435, but until 1910 Congress had increased the number of its members 13 times. In 1910, each district had 211,000 constituents. In 2020, the 435 representatives were obliged to meet the needs of 762,000 constituents—a 360 percent increase. That number is projected to grow to 874,000 by 2040.

In 2021, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences recommended increasing House membership to 585. Its bipartisan study was led by conservative scholar Yuval Levin and liberal congressional expert Norman Ornstein. Their report notes that House members each represent far more constituents than in other populous democracies and that “the United States is the only Western democracy that does not regularly adjust the size of its lower legislative chamber.”

Finally, and most important, America’s state-centric system does in practical fact reliably respect national popular majorities. Critics complain that in the 60 presidential elections since the Constitution took effect in 1789, four times candidates with popular-vote majorities were trumped by electoral vote winners—in 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016. But even that quite low number is at least twice too high. The 1876 electoral—and popular—votes were infamously overridden by an ersatz presidential commission that arbitrarily “awarded” 22 electoral votes to Republican Rutherford B. Hayes from four states in which the popular vote was disputed (three of them former Confederate states), as a notoriously corrupt bargain for Hayes’s promise to withdraw federal troops from the South, thus ushering in the racist Jim Crow state terror regime.

Likewise, the 2000 decision to hand the White House to George W. Bush was not made by the Electoral College electors but by five Republican Supreme Court appointees, who aborted a recount of Florida’s popular votes, by overturning a Florida state Supreme Court order. Bush v. Gore’s unprecedented rejection of state judicial authority was so redolent with raw partisan activism that the Republican justices themselves attempted to deny it any precedential status, calling their “consideration limited to the present circumstances.”

In a system for managing any process as complex as picking the leader of a huge continental nation, 58 out of 60—96.7 percent—is as near perfection as anyone could reasonably expect. It provides Americans with presidents selected by a majority of individual votes nationwide, without unleashing those presidents to turn their country into a massive, or at least an irretrievable, banana republic. The backers of the NPVIC are undoubtedly well intentioned; they certainly aspire to firm up the nation’s democratic foundations. But the compact is unconstitutional and unworkable, and the time spent debating its soundness will only serve to undermine the constitutional order, which, despite our recent Trumpian disruption, is too sturdy and reliable to overthrow.

items.title: This Should Be the First Target of the Democratic Congress
items.content_text:
After one of the most historic victories in American political history, the Democrats will arrive in Congress next January with majorities in both the House and Senate—giving them legislative oversight of federal policy. So the political commentariat has been abuzz over how Democrats will respond to—and rein in—the Trump administration.

Democratic victories are not just a rebuke of the Trump administration’s policies, they also send a clear signal from voters that Democrats can and should confront Trump and his enablers head-on. Incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia caught the spirit of the moment when he sent a two-word tweet to the White House: “Lawyer Up.” Americans are feeling it, as well: According to Pew Research’s November 18 study, eight in 10 Americans are happy with the midterm results and believe Democrats will have a better plan for the future.

The Trump White House responded to the midterm results with as much grace as a car crash in slow motion. On November 9, White House counsel William O. Scharf sent Garcia and several other Democrats a preemptive warning letter stating that Trump “expects members of Congress to discharge their instigative [sic] functions within settled constitutional limits.” If the new Democratic Congress acts within the same kind of “settled constitutional limits” as the current administration, then buckle up for a dizzying 2027.

There are many issues for congressional Democrats to address: the unconstitutional war with Iran, tariffs, rampant inflation, executive overreach, the Supreme Court, and the future of AI. While all of these issues are pressing, Democrats should make investigating immigration officials a top priority. Among the many issues that pushed Democrats to victory this month, the Trump administration’s cruel persecution of immigrants and their families resonated greatly with voters.

Despite the election results, the Trump administration has continued arrests and deportations at its regular pace. Within the past days, a number of ICE arrests have grabbed headlines. On November 20, Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained Chinese-born neuroscientist Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student at Princeton, at Reagan Washington National Airport after she returned from a conference. Xie, who came to the U.S. from China as a child in 2016 and had applied for asylum and been assigned a court hearing in 2028, was detained on the grounds of overstaying a visa. An immigration judge, Anthony Trenga, has ordered ICE to comply with a petition of habeas corpus submitted by Xie’s attorneys, as reported on Friday by The Daily Princetonian.

Domestic flights at airports in other parts of the country have also become a new venue for Trump’s disturbing deportation scheme. In a more brazen act, ICE agents disrupted holiday travel at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday, November 21, when several unmarked agents seized a passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight. The Department of Homeland Security later confirmed that several agents detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, who they asserted had overstayed a visa. ICE then detained Mendoza’s daughter, who threw coffee at the agents as he was taken to custody, and charged her with overstaying a visa, as well. ICE’s actions led Washington Governor Bob Ferguson to call for ICE to be excluded from the state.

In places like California’s San Joaquin Valley, ICE agents continue to detain and deport lifelong residents like Luis Arreguin, who spent 49 of the 54 years of his life in California. For much of the two years since Trump returned to office, ICE and Customs and Border Protection have terrorized communities in the valley, leaving them with empty streets, shells of their former activity.

And, lest we forget, in many of the ICE and Border Patrol sweeps since January 2025, it is U.S. citizens who have been detained, with little thought given to their constitutional rights. ProPublica’s Nicole Foy, who last year broke the first story that ICE had detained 170 U.S. citizens, last month reported that the figure is now closer to 500.

The promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff is proof that, in spite of the midterm gains for Democrats, Trump will likely double down on immigration enforcement. Given Miller’s central role in DHS’s body count policy—arresting people to fill preestablished quotas, even if suspects turned out to be U.S. citizens—along with his documented obsession with pseudo-history and advocacy of the so-called “great replacement theory,” Miller’s new role is a strong signal of the administration’s priorities: Trump essentially views the Republicans’ midterm massacre as an occasion to double down on whatever policies he has in mind to deter future immigration and punish critics of ICE.

If Democrats want to honor their commitment to voters—and really demonstrate plans for a long-term solution for ethical immigration—they will prioritize investigations of the Department of Homeland Security in the coming year.

House and Senate Democrats have hardly been idle while in the minority. As I wrote a year ago, Representative Robert Garcia notably held hearings in Los Angeles regarding the unlawful deployment of the National Guard and the impact of ICE raids on California. On November 2 of this year, ProPublica reported on a letter submitted by a delegation of 40 House Democrats led by Representative Lou Carrera, who demanded that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin release data on the number of U.S. citizens detained by ICE and CBP.

At the moment, Democrats are still developing a strategy for the new year. Politico reported that, despite Trump’s appointing Miller to chief of staff, many congressional Democrats see the midterm results as leverage with Trump to push immigration reform. Several Texas Democrats, including Representative Henry Cuellar and the newly elected Senator James Talarico, have stated they would be willing to work with the Trump administration on real immigration reform.

Much of that logic is rooted in a long-game strategy to push the White House to tone down mass raids and collaborate on new immigration legislation. Part of it is driven by the hope that Trump’s mind has changed, with some pointing to his statement during the recent 60 Minutes interview that his deportation agenda was “too tough” and promulgated the blue wave. Moderate Democrats are also worried about being portrayed as the “open-border” party—a fear going back to the 2024 election and before.

Nevertheless, calls for bipartisanship will not meet the urgent moment. The existing immigration system is so connected with the Trump machine that mere reforms are no match for the horrifying reality of the situation.

Between now and the 2028 election, Democrats have to work toward holding the current immigration bureaucracy, engineered by Donald Trump, accountable—not just for the sake of scoring political points but to repair the country and restore the rule of law. Despite Congress’s deference to the executive branch for the past two years, now is the time for Congress to flex its legislative power as described in the Constitution.

What steps should Democrats take? First, subpoena current and former Trump administration members involved in devising and enforcing immigration policy, as well as contractors affiliated with immigration projects.

We cannot ignore the urgent fact that there have been dozens of cases of people who have died in ICE detention due to poor condition and abuse from guards. “Start with the people who have died in ICE detention at a pace that is twice the historical average,” says Ann Garcia, senior staff attorney at the National Immigration Project. “Congress should subpoena every one of those records along with every detention center contract and assess where gaps led to death.” This inquiry should target agents who killed suspects during detention, such as David Brouillette, who shot immigrant Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during a vehicle stop, along with agents Jonathan Ross, Raymundo Gutierrez, and Jesus Ochoa, who murdered protesters Alex Pretti and Renée Good.

Representative Jamie Raskin, who is slated to become chair of the House Judiciary Committee in January, has indicated that committee would prioritize restoring oversight over DHS. “Congressional Republicans wrote Trump’s ICE and CBP checks for $210 billion in taxpayer money with absolutely no oversight and no accountability,” says Raskin in a statement to The New Republic. “Predictably, we have seen zero oversight by Congressional Republicans on the killings of innocent people by immigration officers in our streets. We have seen zero oversight by Congressional Republicans on the inhumane treatment and deaths that are occurring in Trump’s mass detention centers around the country.”

Congress must also investigate the financial relationship between the deportation apparatus and the Trump family and its acolytes. It should begin with investigating the operation of Geo Group and CoreCivic, both of which maxed out their contributions to Trump’s campaign in 2024. It should also not be a surprise that the Trump family also owns stock in both companies.

Now both private prison corporations are urging ICE officials to purchase their facilities at inflated prices, before Democrats take control of Congress in January. For example, last month ICE paid CoreCivic $485.6 million for its Appleton, Minnesota, detention facility which, a year before, offered it to the state of Minnesota for $75 million. Last week, ICE purchased the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington, from GEO Group for a similar whopping $453 million. As Ann Garcia explains it: “Most of these jails are run by private companies like GEO Group, which put profit before people. The person now running ICE spent more than a decade as a GEO executive. And at a minimum, Congress has to strip ICE and CBP of the slush fund that has paid for all of their abuse against American communities.”

Raskin has signaled that finances would be a key issue of future hearings. “This system of financial irresponsibility, bureaucratic indifference, and medical negligence ends in January,” promised Raskin. “When Democrats take control of the House, we will launch all the congressional oversight and accountability work that Republicans have abandoned.”

Second, pass legislation that establishes clear guardrails on DHS, forces ICE and CBP to be transparent, and have both agencies take accountability for any illegal activity.

Already, current Democratic legislators have begun introducing legislation for the next cycle. Senator Andy Kim of New Jersey authored a bill to require the DHS to report any deaths within detention facilities within 30 days, and an immediate notice if a suspect is killed during enforcement operations like traffic stops. In the House, California Representative Lateefah Simon introduced a bill that would set final orders of removal to expire within 10 years for individuals who have been constantly present within the U.S. and have not committed any crime.

But there is more work to be done to protect the vast majority of aliens, who have never been accused of any crime. There is also a need to reform the rules for private bills with regard to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees. As I previously wrote for The New Republic, ICE and CBP have made the rules regarding private bills more restrictive with deportation cases.

Third, Democrats should invest in studying long-term immigration reform. Like Representative Robert Garcia’s hearings from last year, Democrats need to speak with those caught in the immigration system to understand how immigration policy is structured before the government can rebuild it. If Democrats can learn the lessons from failed policies like the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, it can create a better future that offers honest pathways to citizenship.

In the Senate, the main obstacle that awaits Democrats in the new year is the infamous filibuster. Already, as The Hill has reported, the filibuster is weighing on Senate Democrats who are hoping to avoid run-ins with their Republican colleagues on issues like immigration. Progressives, like Senator Jeff Merkley, have called for replacing the current filibuster rules with the talking filibuster—a continuous debate that ends when the filibustering part runs out of steam. More moderate voices, like Chuck Schumer, have urged caution. But, as political scientist Daniel Wirls noted in his 2021 study The Senate: From White Supremacy to Governmental Gridlock, keeping the filibuster has little to do with honoring political traditions: “It’s about political power, not constitutional principle. When push comes to shove, the vast majority of Senators prefer their individual and partisan power over better government.”

There are many questions that will confront Democrats in the coming months beyond the political calculus of winning in 2028. When pundits discussed immigration in 2024, they were happy to talk about it as an important issue but offered little insight on how it should be managed. What they got was an unchecked secret police that not only has detained and deported thousands of immigrants who have obeyed the law, but has even killed protesters and arrested U.S. citizens. They could articulate immigration as an issue but failed to foresee the rise of an ICE deportation machine, third-country deportations, and the Supreme Court legitimizing racial discrimination with Kavanaugh stops.

Democrats in Congress have a busy year ahead of them. Start by repairing the integrity of the nation’s immigration system.

items.title: Trump Nvidia Scandal Worsens as Todd Blanche Presser Backfires Badly
items.content_text: The Nvidia scandal just got worse. Now that Donald Trump pressured Nvidia into retaining leader Jensen Huang, claiming he’d been “exonerated” despite an affair with someone allegedly passing advanced AI to China, reporters sharply questioned Attorney General Todd Blanche about the Justice Department’s role. It went badly. Blanche refused to say whether Huang had been investigated. He dodged questions about Trump’s claims that Huang had been investigated and exonerated. And he was evasive in many other ways too. That means this scandal has now broadened to include how law enforcement is handling it. So we talked to Representative Jamie Raskin, the next chair of the House Judiciary Committee. Raskin explains how Democrats will investigate DOJ’s role in this fiasco, what will happen when Trump and Blanche obstruct, and what this whole story shows about Trump’s undying love of the world’s autocrats and dictators. Raskin also discusses the role of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who reportedly weakened chip-transfer rules in a way that may have benefited his former firm. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: The Army’s Story About the Iowa Lead Azide Detonation Makes No Sense
items.content_text:
On Wednesday morning, the U.S. Army will blow up some 9,600 pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) near Middletown. Federal officials were spotted on Tuesday afternoon canvassing the town, handing out informational flyers and tape to secure windows, doors, and cracks. The Army and public officials have recommended that residents near the site of the blast evacuate and that others in the vicinity stay indoors. Depending on weather patterns, toxic plumes of lead-containing dust could spread as far as 100 miles away and settle onto the ground, crops, and bodies of water, including the Mississippi River, posing risks to humans as well as pets and livestock. Given the unprecedented nature of such a blast, public officials speaking to Iowa Public Radio noted, the full scope of the public health threat will depend on levels of lead concentration on the ground and in the air, which can only be monitored after the detonation has occurred.

In its current, degraded state, the lead azide—now being stored in two earth-covered, steel-reinforced bunkers—would be extraordinarily dangerous to handle and transport, experts seem to agree, and is liable to explode amid dropping temperatures or inclement weather. That sensitivity also prompted officials to rule out potential chemical neutralization, which would require manipulating the drums. Still, several questions remain about how such an explosive situation was allowed to develop and the full scope of the dangers facing residents of Iowa and neighboring states: Who screwed up? What exactly is getting blown up? And what will that mean for the potentially massive numbers of people living downwind of Wednesday’s blast?

The IAAAP, where the lead azide is stored, is one of several government-owned, contractor-operated “GOCO” facilities spawned between World War II and the early Cold War. While owned by the Army, the facility has since 2008 been operated by a civilian contractor called American Ordnance LLC, a subsidiary of the Philadelphia-based defense contractor Day & Zimmermann. Such facilities—part of the Army’s munitions supply chains—tend to exist in rural areas and are staffed mainly by government contractors and Army civilian employees, with relatively few active military personnel on-site.

These contractors and employees have now found themselves in an impossible situation. Dan Kasteza—who once worked as a chemical officer for the U.S. Army, and has written extensively on the branch’s demilitarization programs—told me over email that there is “no safe way” to deal with the materials in question, leaving controlled detonation as the safest, albeit hardly safe at all, option. “The situation is such that a person cannot safely approach the stockpile and there’s no way you can order someone to do it,” he said. “There’s no PPE that exists for such a situation. Even robotics is somewhat speculative because if the whole stockpile goes up in a bang, it’s enough to send a robot flying through the air, possibly in dangerous fragments, just adding fragmentation to the existing hazards. So the whole thing is a ticking time bomb, so to speak.”

Although the Pentagon has well-established protocols for dealing with toxic waste, recent government communications about the ordeal have described the stockpile’s dangerously sorry state as a relatively new problem. The Army has stated that it discovered that the stored material had “partially crystallized, making it increasingly sensitive to friction, shock, and cold winter temperatures” on March 11. But the Army seems to have been aware of issues with its decades-old lead azide stockpile long before then. A 2014 Army press release notes that the Pentagon began developing alternatives to lead azide in 2004, “in response to the Department of Defense’s concerns over a 40-year-old stockpile of lead azide deteriorating at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.” In September 2025—months before officials said they discovered the problem—the Army posted a contracting opportunity for “Lead Azide Neutralization at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant,” which it “anticipated” would be rewarded to American Ordnance LLC. The Army did not respond to a request for comment as to the fate of that contract.

As the private contractor in charge of the Iowa facility, American Ordnance LLC is also tasked with performing “monthly visual inspections” of the areas where lead azide is stored. As recently as 2024, the Des Moines Register pointed out, the company was fined $9,795 by the Occupational Health and Safety Administration for failing to evaluate at least 20 IAAAP workers for exposure to TNT, a human carcinogen.

The facility is headed up by IAAAP Commander Lt. Col. Daniel V. Nosse. His deputy is a civilian, Bill Kehoe, whose job includes coordinating operations with American Ordnance LLC. Kehoe has been at his post since March 23, not long after the lead azide crystallization was discovered. The Army did not respond to comments as to whether his predecessor’s departure had to do with that discovery.
