Acknowledging his unfamiliarity with the particulars of the situation, Kasteza reasoned that the lead azide could have degraded to such a dire extent thanks to the “institutional laxness or the vicissitudes of an aging Army civilian workforce.” In other words, the problem may be the result of lost expertise: “Civil servants have been badly treated by the Trump administration, and it could easily be that the one or two guys who really had a handle as to what was going were forced into early retirement, had enough and quit, or were DOGE’d away.”

Iowans, meanwhile, have been skeptical of the official explanations for the blast, and frustrated by the limited information they’ve been provided. A lawsuit from the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council sought to stop the blast and resulted in the temporary stay that’s now been lifted. “The Army did a very poor job of communicating with the public until we filed the lawsuit,” Wally Taylor, legal chair for the Sierra Club’s Iowa Chapter, told me on Tuesday. “The Army didn’t think they had to care about anybody here.”

In response to the lawsuit and public outrage about the planned detonation, federal and state officials have provided additional information and resources and beefed up safety protocols. The legal proceedings themselves have also highlighted some possibly worrying details about the Pentagon’s plans. A declaration provided to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit by Ranajit Sahu—an expert witness—flagged several areas of concern. In the Army’s Emergency Permit Application to deal with the waste, a section titled “Brief Description of Waste Involved” contains one bullet point describing lead azide and its dangers, including the potential—when heated—for it to produce “lead metal oxides and fumes, hydrazoic acid vapors and nitrogen oxides.” The second of two bullet points in that section, which appears to contain four or five lines of text, was redacted. The Army and the Environmental Protection Agency did not respond to several requests to explain why that section had been redacted or what other sorts of waste were involved.

In Sahu’s declaration, he notes that hydrazoic acid is “highly toxic” and raised concerns that the Army had not provided guidance related to the public health impact of that substance or the unspecified “combustion gases” noted in the Army’s Environmental Assessment for Lead Azide Risk Mitigation. The various resources provided to Iowa residents seem to pertain only to lead particulate matter, identifying the “two primary pathways” for potential harm as lead exposure from breathing in air after the detonation and lead exposure from dust in surfaces. The literature made, it seems, no mention of hydrazoic acid.

As the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant has burst into headlines, so has its history. The Des Moines Register reported on Tuesday that the IAAAP has in decades past manufactured nuclear weapons—a fact unearthed when several workers on the site were diagnosed with non-Hodgkins lymphoma in the 1980s. More than 2,000 workers in Iowa have made claims under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act, set up to compensate individuals who developed various ailments as a result of their work on typically secretive nuclear weapons programs, and exposure to radioactive materials. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has undertaken extensive remediation efforts in Iowa and other sites where those materials have been stored. Speaking to the Register, Michelle Evermore—a senior director at the National Employment Law Project, who interviewed IAAAP workers for her master’s thesis on the history and ongoing health effects of U.S. weapons programs—wanted “to try to reassure Iowans the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers did a good job,” but “feels it is possible some of the old radioactive material from as far back as the 1940s could also wind up in the air and water when the Army detonates the lead azide.”

In a section on Permitted and Prohibited Identification, the EPA’s Emergency Permit for the detonation redacts two lines of text describing what hazardous wastes the Army is permitted to treat. It does specify that the Army is prohibited from treating any material “contaminated with or suspected of being contaminated with” radioactive material, along with herbicides, biological agents, and other dangerous substances.

That it might only be lead-laden dust billowing over a large swath of the United States is hardly comforting. Only diligent testing over the coming days, weeks, and months will be able to determine just how much damage the detonation wrought. Maybe eventually we’ll also get more answers about how hastily blowing up nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide came to be the safest possible solution to a problem decades in the making.

items.title: Judge Rips Into Trump DOJ for Blatant Election Interference Ploy
items.content_text:
A federal judge determined Tuesday that the Justice Department intentionally rushed charges against a pair of former FBI officials who worked on the Hunter Biden laptop case, all at the behest of Donald Trump.

The DOJ attempted to prosecute former intelligence analyst Nikki Floris, who ran the intelligence division at the Washington Field Office, and Bradley Benavides, a former deputy assistant director for counterintelligence. Both were charged with lying to Congress regarding Biden’s laptop contents. But the case barely had any legs at all and earlier this month was thrown out by U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, who argued at the time that the government’s case was tantamount to “weaponization.”

Faruqui further explained his rationale in a 48-page opinion Tuesday, tying the meritless accusations to Trump’s orders—and the midterm election cycle. A portion of Faruqui’s timeline of events preceding the charges pinpoints a July 16 national address delivered by the president, in which Trump specifically directed the FBI, as well as the CIA and the Justice Department, to investigate and charge people who participated in an alleged “cover-up” during the 2020 presidential election. The following day, FBI Director Kash Patel assigned the case to the Kansas City FBI office.

From Faruqui’s position, “there was no date of legal significance looming that necessitated the urgency of a complaint.”

“However, there was a date on the calendar that cannot be ignored,” Faruqui noted. “The midterm elections.”

“The motive for [the rush to charge] is clear: to appease President Trump in his campaign of retribution against the FBI and to score cheap political points to impact the midterm elections.”

Faruqui blasted the DOJ for compromising on its own values throughout the second Trump administration, arguing that the “slapdash prosecution” of Floris and Benavides is a testament to how far the department has compromised on its self-purported values of “independence and impartiality.”

He also observed that the general public has “suffered” under the administration’s loose approach to law enforcement, writing that “this case is not a one-off mistake” but rather one in a long string of “botched, politicized cases” where the government has rushed to charge, only for the prosecutions to eventually unravel and fall apart. He cited statistics indicating that, over the last 10 years, the government had dismissed just 0.5 percent of the cases charged by criminal complaint, whereas, by comparison, the government moved to dismiss a stunning 21 percent of all cases charged by criminal complaint during the eight-week period in which the National Guard occupied Washington.

“For years, the Administration has treated the weaponization of law enforcement like a horror movie villain coming for them. Now the threat is finally real,” Faruqui concluded. “Only the call is coming from inside the house—the White House. Perhaps, less time on the pool and more on reflecting.”

items.title: Clueless Trump Wants to Bring Back His Most Disastrous Policy
items.content_text:
More tariffs are coming.

The Trump administration is ready to propose a new set of tariffs against the European Union, China, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, and 27 other EU members, according to reporting from The Wall Street Journal. They are expected to be announced by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in the coming days.

These tariffs are meant to be a revised version of the “Liberation Day” tariffs, holding a metaphorical import tax gun to the heads of countries the U.S. has any kind of trade deficit with in exchange for investments that likely won’t do anything to help everyday Americans. Those tariffs were also struck down by the Supreme Court.

China’s upcoming tariff rate won’t be more than 20 percent, the EU’s no more than 15 percent. There will be built-in options to lower those rates if countries move to reduce their own manufacturing industries—at the behest of President Trump. Regardless, these new tariffs are already facing a backlash.

“Donald Trump and JD Vance’s tariffs continue to screw over families, farmers, and small businesses—driving up costs and making life more expensive,” Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro wrote on X Tuesday. “This Administration’s failed economic policies are a disaster for Pennsylvanians—and they just don’t give a damn.”

“We’re going to lose the WH in ’28 because of this. We’ve added less than 10,000 manufacturing jobs and are still about -200,000 what we were in 2023,” conservative commentator John Cardillo said. “All these new tariffs will do is drive prices higher and hurt American companies forced to pay them upfront, as there are no US made alternatives for much of what they’re importing. Trump is crushing American businesses and consumers.”

“Three weeks ago voters told Trump prices were the problem. Now he’s getting ready to bring the tariffs back. He clearly didn’t get the message,” former GOP Congressman Adam Kinzinger wrote Tuesday. “The rates would roughly match last year’s. Countries that cut deals with Trump would pay 15 percent or less, and everyone else would pay more. I’m not against trade enforcement. But we already tried this, and it led to higher prices for all of us. The importers got refunds and we got stuck with the costs.”

Tariffs are one of the primary reasons voters gave for abandoning Trump and the GOP in the midterm elections, as price hikes on daily goods like meat, appliances, and automobiles negatively impacted millions of Americans. His return to them is questionable, to say the least.

items.title: Trump Uses Turkey Pardon Speech to Cry Election Fraud
items.content_text:
The presidential turkey pardon is a silly, annual Thanksgiving tradition that spares the lives of a pair of turkeys and, more importantly, sets the celebratory tone ahead of one of America’s biggest national holidays. Donald Trump’s 2026 variation of the typically delightful ceremony was anything but.

Instead, the president used the opportunity at the lectern on the White House South Lawn Tuesday to address the American public for the umpteenth time about his myriad construction projects, including his half-finished ballroom, and supposed midterm election fraud.

“I’m pleased to report that the price of gasoline also has dropped 20 percent in the last two weeks. You notice it dropped right after the election? I wonder if someone had that in mind. A little strange,” Trump said.

Gas has dropped nearly 90 cents over the past two months, a welcome reprieve following months of rising prices due to the Iran war. The underlying reason has several contributing factors, ranging from increased oil flow out of the Middle East (including through the Strait of Hormuz), Trump’s diminished warmongering rhetoric, and anticipated seasonal price adjustments on the cusp of winter.

But the president apparently has not interpreted the deflated costs as an achievement of his administration, but rather a post-midterm conspiracy cooked up by his perceived political enemies.

“That happened with the Covid vaccine, right? Right after the election they announced we had a Covid vaccine,” Trump mused—referring to the results of the rapid vaccine development program during his first administration, which hit the market in December 2020—before immediately unraveling his own point. “But I actually announced it a few days before so I can’t blame them too much for that.”

For nearly 20 minutes, Trump prattled to the American public about his various mental fixations before eventually ceding the floor to this year’s two birds: Freedom and Feathers (whose names Trump promptly insulted).

items.title: Trump Thinking About Assassinating Iranian Leaders
items.content_text:
President Trump is ready to reignite his flailing forever war in Iran.

NBC News reports that the Trump administration is currently weighing whether or not to carry out assassination attempts against high-ranking Iranian leaders, an option that some in the White House think could end the war rather than intensify it. This comes as Trump has been claiming that the war was won for weeks—a narrative that no one seems to be buying based on the outcome of the midterm election.

“The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. The president has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Operation Iron Gate … will continue with full effect,” an administration official told NBC. “President Trump has many options at his disposal and will make the best possible decision to ensure Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon.”

The war on Iran started with the assassination of a high-ranking leader—Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. That led to more aggression from Iran, not less.

The Pentagon has yet to comment.

items.title: Todd Blanche Admits He Won’t Investigate Potential Espionage
items.content_text:
The head of the Justice Department insists he doesn’t even know what he’d investigate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for.

Attorney General Todd Blanche deflected from a simple question about the chip maker during a DOJ press conference Tuesday, claiming to not even understand the premise of why he’d examine Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

“Had Huang been investigated?” asked a reporter.

The simple question was enough to send Blanche over the edge.

“I’m not going to talk about investigation. What does that mean? ‘Had Huang been investigated?’ For what? But you can’t just—I don’t understand the question,” Blanche spat back. “The reporting from the various sources or leaks or whatever was out there didn’t suggest that Huang himself was under some sort of investigation, at least not that I saw.

“But it’s not fair to the process, it’s certainly not fair to him, to speculate about things or answer hypothetical questions, so no,” said the top man at America’s key law enforcement agency.

Huang resumed his roles as Nvidia’s president, chief executive officer, and member of the board on Monday, mere days after he had been tossed out of the company he co-founded over revelations of his numerous extramarital affairs, the most dubious of which involved a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies identified as a spy and a state asset. The paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation of Jensen’s), had reportedly been in contact with an officer from China’s Ministry of State Security throughout her affair with the Nvidia chief.

The board of directors said that their decision to reinstate Huang and ignore the national security concerns surrounding the billionaire’s activities were based on influential conversations with “senior levels of the United States government.” Hours later, Donald Trump phoned in to CNBC to take credit, revealing that he personally assured the board both “directly and indirectly” that Huang was not a national security risk.

Blanche’s outright dismissal of a possible investigation appears to be in line with the White House, which seems keen to brush Huang’s scandal under the rug so long as he keeps making money.

Nvidia shares spiraled in the weeks after Huang was ousted from the company, rattling the U.S. economy and Trump’s personal stock portfolio with it: The president’s 2026 financial disclosures revealed that he purchased between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock earlier this year. As of September 30, Trump was believed to have 370,000 shares in Nvidia, according to a review by the Financial Times. Huang’s unexpected reappointment sent the company’s stock skyrocketing, jumping by 31.5 percent and adding some $950 billion to the company’s overall value. Trump, for his part, made up to $15 million, reported the Financial Times.

items.title: Trump Sec. Says She’ll Fight to Keep Sending Weird Religious Emails
items.content_text:
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins clearly doesn’t understand the First Amendment.

The devout Christian told Fox News Tuesday that she plans to appeal a recent judicial decision that deemed her Jesus-laden, agency-wide messages unconstitutional.

“We’re gonna fight it all the way to the Supreme Court,” Rollins said. “Obviously our Constitution—it’s not freedom from religion, it’s freedom of religion.

“Democrats and Republicans through the decades have relied on their faith. As a leader in this country, I’ll never stop doing that,” she added.

At issue was an incredibly on-the-nose email Rollins sent on April 5 commemorating Easter.

“Happy Easter—He is Risen indeed!” Rollins wrote to some 100,000 staffers at the Department of Agriculture from her official government email address at the time. “Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind.

“And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for.”

But her proselytizing was far from kosher. Last week, U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco ruled that Rollins’s messages violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause, as Rollins had not only used her position to assume that Christianity was the shared faith of USDA workers but also had effectively leveraged her position within the federal government to spread the word of Jesus. In doing so, Rollins blatantly violated a USDA memorandum on religious expression in the workplace that passed under her purview.

Citing language from the memorandum, Thompson declared that Rollins “cannot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances,” “cannot use official authority to pressure subordinates,” and must stop if a colleague requests she do so.

But the note was just one of many breaches by the Trump administration of America’s long-standing religious freedom. Weeks into his second term, Donald Trump signed an executive order establishing the official White House Faith Office, led by televangelist pastor Paula White-Cain. That same week, Trump issued another executive order to “end the anti-Christian weaponization of government.”

Months later, in July, the Office of Personnel Management issued a similar memo, effectively allowing federal employees to attempt to convert their colleagues in the workplace and encourage them to pray in the workplace. The Department of Labor also established its own faith office, where its religious leader, Kenneth Wolfe, hosts monthly worship services.

The evangelical effusions have been unabashed and shameless. In January, the niece of Martin Luther King Jr. and the senior adviser on faith and community outreach at USDA—Alveda King—told DOL employees that “we have different denominations, different faiths, and some have no faith.”

“Those are the ones I would be more concerned about,” King emphasized.

In March, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Americans to pray “every day” on their knees “in the name of Jesus Christ.” Government employees have disclosed that the hyperfixation on Christianity has made the federal government a very uncomfortable place to work, spurring an environment in which staffers fear religion-based retaliation.

items.title: Senate Republicans, Led By Thune, Are Sticking With Trump
items.content_text:
Future Republican Senate Minority Leader John Thune is prepared to “rebuild” his party while carrying out the Trump administration agenda that lost it the midterms.

“We got our butts kicked, and you’ve got to learn from that and rebuild and get better,” the South Dakota senator said in an interview with Semafor, released Tuesday, referring to the GOP’s midterm election losses. “We’ve got a governing coalition out there waiting to happen, but we’ve got to start talking to them.”

Thune hinted that the new Republican Senate might be more keen on reining in the president’s new failed forever war in Iran.

“Most of our members have tried to give the president a lot of latitude on managing the situation in Iran … but that’s I think an issue where people are probably going to be more inclined going forward to maybe have their own position on it,” he said.

While Thune has feuded with Trump in the past—particularly on the passage of the SAVE America Act—his seriousness about ending the war remains to be seen. Last week, Senate Republicans still voted to block a war powers resolution to force Trump to end the conflict with Iran or seek Congress’s permission.

Besides that, Thune’s new plan seems to be eerily similar to the old one. He wants to keep work requirements for Medicaid, has no problem with 93-year old Senator Chuck Grassley running again, and has no intention of working across the aisle on anything other than AI regulation—even as he has the opportunity to pull the party back from the MAGA era.

items.title: Investigating Nvidia Just Shot Way Up on Dems’ Priority List
items.content_text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.


Inside Washington

Following Monday’s stunning news that Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, congressional Democrats scrambled to move the company higher up on their list of oversight priorities come January. House and Senate Democrats, including those who would be most important in a potential investigation, issued a flurry of statements on the news, raising concerns about everything from national security to chip exports to President Donald Trump’s involvement in Huang’s comeback. (The president reportedly called into Nvidia’s board meeting on Sunday to advocate for Huang’s return.)

Huang resigned from Nvidia on November 12 following reports that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, as well as two Nvidia employees. Alice Huang was allegedly in contact with China’s spy agency throughout her affair with Jensen Huang, raising concerns that their relationship was part of a plan to funnel Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China through Megaspeed, circumventing U.S. export controls.

“Yet another example where, in Trump’s America, the wealthy and well connected are held to a different standard. We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO and why his administration failed to restrict the PRC’s access to our most sensitive technology,” Representative Gregory Meeks wrote in a statement. Meeks is the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, one of the bodies that Huang promised on November 17 to testify privately in front of. Those closed-door hearings are expected to continue as planned.

Huang also agreed to testify privately before the House Intelligence Committee and the House China Select Committee. He will testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3 in a hearing called “Protecting America’s AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls.” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking member of the committee, focused on export controls in her statement. “Jensen Huang’s return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk,” she wrote.

Polling suggests that Americans aren’t fans of Nvidia’s business practices. In an online poll of 1,000 voters conducted last week, Demand Progress and YouGov Blue found that 73 percent support an investigation into whether Nvidia’s chips reached China, and 64 percent want to pause the company’s sales of advanced chips to buyers in China. Respondents were also concerned about Nvidia’s size and dominance over the chip industry—65 percent said they think Nvidia’s control of the market puts the United States at risk.

Outrage over Huang’s misconduct and reinstatement has given China hawks an opening to advocate for more export controls on AI chips. Some Democrats, including Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries, are calling for action as soon as mid-December through the National Defense Authorization Act, an annual bill that funds the Defense Department. “The National Defense Authorization Act must include ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries,” Jeffries wrote in a statement on Monday. “It’s time for traditional Republicans in Congress to join us in reining in this corruption.”

Compared to other tech companies like Meta, Palantir, and OpenAI, Nvidia has largely flown under congressional Democrats’ radar, explained Colin McGlynn, the AI policy adviser for Demand Progress. In part, that’s because some progressives aren’t fully comfortable with conservative and centrist critiques of Nvidia. “I think that part of the reason it’s been hard to get progressives and corporate power people on board with this is because they don’t love the China hawk framing of this.”

But the messaging from Democrats on Monday suggests that there will be plenty of other reasons for Congress to investigate Nvidia in the new year. “Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough, and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,” Jeffries also wrote in his statement, suggesting that Dems could tie any investigations of Nvidia into their broader anti-corruption oversight agenda.

“No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions. Congress must come together in swift bipartisan action and demand answers immediately,” wrote Representative Robert Garcia, the ranking member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. Garcia will lead Democrats’ efforts to investigate the Trump administration and its corporate allies next year.

 “I’ve been raising concerns for months about the president’s decision to allow NVIDIA to sell advanced chips to China, as well as the convenient timing of the president’s NVIDIA stock purchases. We must demand a full accounting of who knew what and when,” Represenative Johnny Olszewski, who serves on the Subcommittee on East Asia and Pacific under Foreign Affairs, told The TNR Blue Book. “I’m confident that Committee Democrats are fully aligned in our commitment to investigate both the corruption of the Administration and its national security implications.”

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

The strangest story of the past week continues. No, not Jensen Huang being reinstated as CEO—although that sure is weird. We’re talking about the U.S. Army apparently backing itself into a corner in which it must explode 68 barrels of lead azide near Middletown, Iowa, on short notice, dropping toxic lead dust on communities as far as 100 miles away or more. (Middletown is in the southeast corner of the state not far from the Mississippi.) This story started back in March, when a “routine stockpile surveillance operation” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant discovered a bunch of lead azide that had been degrading in a bunker for decades, putting it at a risk of exploding. At first, The New York Times recently revealed, the Trump administration hired a firm to “safely dissolve the chemicals,” before canceling the contract two months later. The administration didn’t respond to the paper’s questions about this or questions about why the lead azide had been moldering in a bunker for this long to begin with.

The Environmental Protection Agency then issued a permit for detonation, which was stayed last week by the U.S. Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals after environmental groups said the EPA hadn’t followed proper procedure. Then the Army said over the weekend that it would use emergency powers to detonate the lead this week anyway, because temperatures under 30 degrees could lead the materials to explode on its own. From Brian Smith’s report for The Des Moines Register: “The bunkers housing the barrels are more susceptible to temperature swings now because the blast doors were removed in preparation for the detonation and cannot be replaced.” Donald Trump on Monday, in a lengthy Truth Social post, blamed the whole situation on the Obama administration and said Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat, would need to agree to “the operation.”

Sand isn’t in office yet, so it’s not clear what he has to do with all this. Current (Republican) Governor Kim Reynolds has meanwhile set up a website with information on the planned detonation—although good luck finding user-friendly information on how things got to this point or how much nearby communities need to worry about the lead dust. The site does link to a vague 500-word summary from the military promising that it will use water mist to knock lead dust out of the air and engage in “cleanup actions where needed.” An appeals court gave the detonation the go-ahead on Monday afternoon. It’s currently scheduled for Wednesday.

Elsewhere:

  • While much of the country prepares for Thanksgiving (and its associated travel tie-ups), California, and particularly the northern section of the state, is bracing for a powerful one-two punch from especially high king tides plus surge from a Tuesday storm. The city of San Francisco has been handing out sand bags, according to the San Francisco Chronicle, which also reports San Francisco Public Works spokesperson Rachel Gordon asking people to sweep up leaves to avoid clogging storm drains and to look after their neighbors. (The paper’s personal finance columnist, Jessica Roy, recently urged readers to prepare for El Niño season by taking a video walkthrough of their home for insurance documentation purposes.) California Governor Gavin Newsom already declared an emergency back in September, due to forecasters warning about the intersection of the king tides with higher rain totals and sea levels from El Niño. The sandbags, sand berms, rock, pumps, and further resources made ready in the wake of that decision are about to be tested. And the season is young.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

At the Center for American Progress, Kalina Gibson, Jasia Smith, and Margaret Cooney list “5 Ways the Trump Administration Will Make It Harder for Americans to Weather El-Niño-Driven Food Insecurity.” At the top of their list, unsurprisingly, is SNAP cuts and the defunding of climate-smart agriculture programs. But they also argue that the war on Iran, cuts to weather and climate monitoring, and chaotic trade policy will exacerbate price spikes, instability, and supply chain disruption.

The Revolving Door Project has thoughts on the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. “Nvidia’s Board of Directors should be treated as persona non grata,” RDP executive director Jeff Hauser said in a press release quickly published on the organization’s website after news of Huang’s reinstatement broke. “Every trade association that retains Nvidia as a member should be frozen out. All Nvidia lobbyists who do not quit should be forever shunned.” Hauser then reiterated the organization’s support for a ban on individual stock ownership for individuals serving in Congress.

SIn case you missed it: Last week, the Century Foundation published a post-midterm analysis suggesting that household debt was a much bigger deal in this election than previously reported. “Two-thirds (68 percent) of midterm voters carrying debt said that their household debt motivated them to vote,” Julie Margetta Morgan, Mike Pierce, and Alex Edwards wrote, “with 40 percent saying it motivated them ‘a lot.’”

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Four Questions For: Suzanne Mettler, professor of government at Cornell University and academic director of the Scholars Strategy Network

Q: Who are you, and what are you working on right now? 

A: I’m a political scientist who studies American politics. My most recent book with Trevor E. Brown, Rural Versus Urban: The Growing Divide That Threatens Democracy, examined the sources of the rural-urban political divide, and now I’m studying what can help reduce it. I’m focusing particularly on what can help rural areas gain meaningful party competition, fostering greater accountability, and responsiveness to rural needs.

Q:  How does your work help us understand the latest midterm elections?

A: The midterm elections became a blue wave because the Democratic Party successfully moderated the rural-urban divide, gaining a higher percentage of the vote in less populated places than it has in many years or even decades. Of the nine U.S. Senate seats Democrats flipped, all but one are in states with a higher than average percentage of rural residents, and rural counties that flipped in those states contributed to the outcomes. In elections for the U.S. House of Representatives in rural districts, Democratic candidates flipped 22 seats and Democratic incumbents won reelection in all but one.

Q: What is the most striking thing you’ve found in your recent work?

A: I’m fascinated by the individuals who ran as Democratic candidates in many rural places this year, both those who won and those who lost but over-performed. Certainly they had national winds at their backs, but that alone can’t explain their success. Many of them are particularly well suited, by their own backgrounds, to represent their communities well, and they worked hard to build bridges in places where the Democratic Party has long been largely rejected by voters as a viable alternative.

Q: What keeps you going in these stressful times?

A: The midterms offer hope that the political polarization and extremism spurred by the rural-urban divide, which has been so damaging to our politics, can be diffused. Americans broadly, across both rural and urban counties, expressed concern about many of the same issues, and they moved in tandem in support of change. If a rural-urban governing coalition can be forged, government can respond to Americans’ needs regardless of where they live.

Interview by Monica Potts


Political Trivia Question of the Day  

Which president made the custom of pardoning a Thanksgiving turkey official? (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: De Niro, Fonda Back Chris Van Hollen For Senate Majority Leader
items.content_text:
Chuck Schumer has lost Jane Fonda and Robert De Niro.

A group of about 35 celebrities and donors released a letter on Tuesday calling for Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, not New York Senator Schumer, to lead the party as Senate majority leader. The signees include Fonda, De Niro, Chelsea Handler, Marisa Tomei, Padma Lakshmi, former BlackRock executive Morris Pearl, The Vagina Monologues writer V, and Veep creator David Mandel.

“This is an opportunity. This is a window,” Handler told The New York Times. “We need to, like, get the ball and run with it. And I don’t believe that Chuck Schumer is going to do that.”

“Americans voted for the change necessary to fight the corruption, cruelty and policies of Trump and his Epstein-class cronies,” De Niro wrote in a statement. “That’s why I’m supporting change in Senate leadership … [Senator Van Hollen is] a fierce fighter.”

The letter also called for a transparent, open-door vote for the leadership.

“The Senate Democratic leader will be chosen behind closed doors, by secret ballot,” the letter read. “No senator will ever have to tell voters, or us, how they voted. We believe a decision this consequential deserves public accountability.”

Calls for Van Hollen to replace Schumer—who is still presumed to be in the lead for the leadership—have spiked post-midterms, as voters, donors, and colleagues point to Schumer’s loyalty to the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee, Israel, corporate PACs, his commitment to moderation (perhaps best displayed in his refusal to endorse New York’s Democratic Socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani), and his old age (76) as reasons to choose Van Hollen. The Maryland senator has carved out a reputation for progressive stands in Trump’s second tenure, as Handler pointed to his trip to El Salvador on behalf of the wrongly deported Kilmar Ábrego García.

Senators Bernie Sanders, Jeff Merkley, and Elissa Slotkin, as well as Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed, have all come out against Schumer.

The vote to decide who will lead Senate Democrats is scheduled for December 1.

items.title: No One Wants to Work With Kash Patel
items.content_text:
The FBI is bleeding staff under Kash Patel’s leadership.

Christopher Raia, the bureau’s deputy director, is expected to retire by the year’s end, according to several insiders that spoke to The Washington Post.

Raia, 50, joined the FBI as a special agent in 2003. In January, he was tapped to replace conservative podcaster Dan Bongino to run day-to-day operations for the FBI. Bongino left at the start of the year. Andrew Bailey, Bongino’s co-deputy director (a never-before-seen role apparently invented specifically because of Bongino), resigned in September.

By the time Raia exits the bureau in December, he will have manned the agency for less than a year. The FBI did not respond to the Post’s request for comment about Raia’s expected retirement.

But Raia will just be another innumerable loss for the national law investigative agency. Since Donald Trump returned to office, the bureau is down at least 1,500 special agents. Their exits have mostly been fueled by firings, forced layoffs, or buyouts. Some were swept away by staffing purges that sought to make the FBI more loyal to Trump—such as firing the agents who investigated the Trump-fueled riot at the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021—while others were stripped of their positions to remove friction from the increasingly MAGA environment.

And Patel, himself, has been far from a bastion of excellence during his time atop the bureau. Over the last year, the podcaster turned agency chief has wantonly flown around the country with FBI jets on the taxpayer’s dime. His trips have included a jaunt to Las Vegas, a trip to Nashville, and at least one widely publicized instance in which he flew to Penn State to visit his then-girlfriend (now fiancée), country singer Alexis Wilkins.

Patel’s alleged substance abuse issues have also caused problems: The FBI director ruffled feathers when he appeared at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan, where he was caught on video chugging beer and whooping it up with the U.S. men’s hockey team. (He later insisted that he was celebrating with his “friends.”) He has also reportedly delayed meetings and time-sensitive operations and often been unreachable due to drinking, raising concerns about the potential for foreign coercion and other national security risks.

In April, a federal judge threw out Patel’s defamation claims against a former FBI official, Frank Figliuzzi, who told MS NOW that Patel had “been visible at nightclubs far more” than he had been seen on the seventh floor of the bureau’s Washington headquarters.

items.title: Here’s How Much Bank Trump Made From Bringing Back Jensen Huang
items.content_text:
President Trump has made up to $15 million on Nvidia stock after Jensen Huang made his return as CEO—a move Trump himself had a major role in orchestrating.

Huang was removed as Nvidia CEO less than a week ago after it was revealed that he was having affairs with multiple women, one of whom was identified as a Chinese spy by the Trump administration’s intelligence. Days later, the company’s board of directors brought him back because they “received input from senior levels of the United States government.”

Trump bragged openly about providing that input in a 50-minute interview with CNBC on Monday, speaking excitedly about how it turned the entire market around.

“I watched the screen.… Now it’s a rocket ship going in the right direction,” he said. “And it’s saving the whole market.… It could be that there’s never been anything like it.”

Trump’s excitement may be based in the fact that he’s been trading Nvidia stock, and owned as much as 370,000 shares in Nvidia as of September 30—making his role in Huang’s return all the more questionable, as he is making money off of a company whose profit is directly related to his personal and political decisions as president.

Nvidia’s stock price shares shot up by 31.5 percent on Monday in reaction to Huang’s return, adding a whopping $950 billion in value to the company.

“I think it’s worth being candid about what happened here,” The Bulwark’s Sam Stein wrote on X Monday. “The US government pressured the board of a private company to reinstate a CEO who had compromised US national security and broken serious internal HR policies because they liked what he did to the share price.”

Democratic calls for investigation have begun.

“The Trump Administration’s rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act. Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Senator Chuck Schumer wrote online. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”

“Jensen Huang compromised our national security, and yet he was reinstated to his old position because the President of the United States asked for it. The same President who owns millions of dollars of Nvidia stock that rebounded after the reinstatement,” Representative Pramila Jayapal wrote. “This is unacceptable and reeks of corruption. Congress will investigate.”

items.title: Transcript: Trump’s New Nvidia Spin Instantly Wrecked by Damning Leaks
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 24 episode of The Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

In an extraordinary turn in the Nvidia scandal, its leader, Jensen Huang, has been reinstated after direct intervention from Donald Trump and top officials in the U.S. government. Trump openly flaunted this in an interview with CNBC, stating straight out that he’d pressured Nvidia’s board to rehire Huang, even though U.S. intelligence had previously raised alarms about his affair with a possible Chinese honeypot. What’s striking is that even as Trump did this, The New York Times was breaking another story based on leaked intelligence that Huang’s partner in the affair was in direct contact with senior Chinese intelligence, undermining Trump’s assurances about Huang.

We really like the take on this offered by Adam Gurri, the publisher of Liberal Currents, who argued that this saga underscores the need for the new Democratic Congress to go very hard at Trump corruption and elite corruption. So we’re talking to him now. Adam, thanks for coming on.

Adam Gurri: Thank you for having me.

Sargent: Quick recap. Jensen Huang got pushed out as leader of Nvidia after it was reported that he’d had an affair with a woman who appeared to be passing AI intelligence to China. Trump knew about that but did nothing.

Now Huang’s been reinstated after Trump pushed Nvidia’s board to do so. Nvidia itself announced that on this decision it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government.” 

Adam, they “received input.”  What do you think that means, and what’s your quick reaction to this latest turn?

Gurri: I think it’s just another case of elite impunity. You know, it seemed like such a good turn that they actually fired him, because that happens so little these days with corporate boards. So it was encouraging to actually see some kind of accountability, but they backtracked almost immediately.

I think probably because the Trump administration and the other tech people that were lobbying for this, they don’t like seeing accountability, particularly. And they do like stocks going up.

Sargent: Yes, that’s exactly what seems to have happened. Trump wanted the stock to keep going up. So let’s listen to Trump talk about this on CNBC. Here he’s confirming right out in the open that he directly pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang.

Donald Trump (voiceover): Well, I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it. And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was, to me, a very important part of our country. This is, you know, it represents something very special, what he’s done and what the company’s done. And I found the board to be very, very reasonable.

Sargent: And here’s Trump confirming that he and other officials assured Nvidia’s board that Jensen Huang posed no national security threat, despite everything they knew about Jensen and his affair.

Trump (voiceover): And they came back and they did the right thing. That was not an easy thing to do. But they did ask for assurance on the national security threat, and we gave him assurance, at least with everything we know, and we know a lot. So with everything we know, we gave him assurance.

Sargent: Adam, the core problem here seems to be that we have no way of knowing whether it’s actually true that top officials don’t see this whole affair as a threat, because Trump himself is so compromised, right? There’s no reason to suspect that he has the national interest in mind in any sense. This is shockingly corrupt, isn’t it?

Gurri: It is. And it’s just laughable how this administration always postures itself as the China hawk ones in our party system, whereas Joe Biden actually banned the selling of chips to China and actually enforced it. It’s the same thing with the tariffs. It’s the same thing with everything.

If there’s money to be had, enforcement is a matter of negotiation. You know, so one of the reasons, for example, that the tariffs haven’t hit as hard as they could have on paper is because there’s a lot of backroom deals that go on to get exceptions and things like that. And it’s similar here.

Obviously the chip ban was already in place. They claim to be for it and to be strong on China. But really they’re stronger on, like, Canada and the EU in practice than they are on China.

Sargent: So even as Trump was urging Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, the New York Times broke another big story on this. The Times reported that Huang’s mistress, whose name is Alice Huang, no relation, was regularly in contact with a senior Chinese spy during the affair. This is how U.S. intelligence came to suspect that this was a honeypot operation targeting Jensen.

And the latest Times piece is based on leaks from people who have seen U.S. intelligence reports on this whole thing. The fact that senior U.S. government people are apparently leaking this is itself important.

It directly undercuts Trump’s rationale for pushing Huang back and seems designed to alert the public that something might be seriously amiss here.

Clearly Trump sees in Jensen Huang a mirror image of himself in some sense. And once Trump has imprinted in that way, like, all bets are off, right? Like, the national interest is so far from his mind at moments like that that you can’t even—it’s laughable.

Gurri: The clearest lens to look at him through is, he cares first and foremost about his own personal power, and about people bending the knee to him, more than any substantive ideological goal.

He clearly hates immigrants. He clearly actually thinks tariffs work. And he clearly loves money. But that’s the personalism: enriching himself, his own personal power, even if it means weakening the institutions themselves that he exercises the power through.

And then you have a bunch of people that are under him that have their own agendas, and actually care about China, or actually care about deporting people, or whatever it is. And they can fight it out, but what they cannot do is actually call out Trump himself, right?

So Trump himself can step in and say, Huang is my guy. He is going back to Nvidia. I don’t care about this China stuff one way or the other. I don’t even care if it’s true, or to figure out whether it’s true or not. He’s my guy. I want my stocks to go up. He’s, you know, he’s going back. And the anti-China side can retaliate, but they can’t retaliate directly, because to do that is—you’re done. You’re done in Trumpworld.

Sargent: It’s probably worth pointing out as well that Trump was asked during the CNBC interview about the fact that he was briefed by U.S. intelligence some time ago about the risk that this affair that Jensen Huang had posed. Trump’s answer was this: “I won’t get into it.”

Adam, we just do not know anything close to the full range of what Trump’s own U.S. intelligence officials, A, told him about the situation, which he decided to do nothing about, and B, what they’ve actually learned, right?

We don’t know what intelligence has concluded about this affair. So how bad do you think these revelations could get? And is there a way for the Democratic Congress to get to the bottom of this next year?

Gurri: I mean, I strongly suspect that this goes well beyond this one affair and this one bad actor. I really wonder—and even, I think it very likely goes beyond Jensen Huang himself, right? There’s got to be more of Nvidia involved in shady dealings. So, I mean, really, as always, the main thing that Democratic members of Congress can do next year is investigate.

The senator from Arizona, Ruben Gallego, made a statement shortly after Jensen Huang was reinstated, essentially saying that we needed to look into the trades that occurred before this announcement, which I think is a good sign that he’s signaling that. And in general, Democrats have been making noises that they’re going to be going big on oversight. And that is something that they can do in Congress.

But we should not forget that Democrats are not just going to be in Congress. They are in the states, more states than ever now, including many states that Nvidia does business in. Frustratingly, the Democrats already had California and Delaware, pretty much the two most important for Nvidia specifically.

Both of those states can do a lot to investigate, especially Delaware, given that’s where they’re incorporated. So I think that’s where the most impactful actions can be taken. In Congress, the main thing they can do is investigate and share the findings of their investigation with both the public and prosecutors at the state level.

Sargent: And as you pointed out a little earlier in this discussion, Nvidia’s board did the right thing at the outset when they removed Jensen Huang, which was actually a sign of a positive push toward something like accountability for an elite.

And so the fact that Nvidia has now turned 180 degrees and just done what Trump has essentially told them to do really strikes me as a very major backslide for the prospects for elite accountability. That’s your argument. Can you talk about that?

Gurri: Yeah, so I think everyone remembers last year, at the beginning of the year in particular, it was just like elite institutions were caving one by one. They were treating the 2024 election like it was the 1984 election where Reagan won all but 13 electoral votes, when it really was not.

It was just another one of our polarized-era elections, where one side won by a coin toss, in a favorable environment, essentially. Anyway, they all caved then.

What’s crazy is, Democrats just won a midterm like we have not seen in something like 50 years. If anything, there’s the analogy with 1984. But still, Nvidia is clearly still afraid of what the Trump administration could do for the next two years, which is, they can definitely do a lot. Or unafraid of what Democrats will do, because Democrats haven’t credibly shown that they’re willing to punch back.

Biden’s whole approach was mostly just, let’s move on. You know, they sort of grudgingly started investigating and prosecuting Trump for some very obvious crimes, too slowly. They were very quick to move on, like, low-level January 6 guys, showing that they could move quickly if they were motivated. But mostly they were reticent, too, for understandable reasons.

But we’re just so far beyond that. We’re so far beyond that. And because they’ve shown that reticence, you know, I don’t think Elon Musk actually thinks that anything bad is going to happen as a result of this election. He’s still just talking like that was so silly of me to spend all that money in Texas. And certainly I think the Nvidia board is much more afraid of Donald Trump than they are of Democrats.

Sargent: When you put it that way, it really bodes very badly, and I think raises the stakes for the Democratic congressional takeover. I really hope Democrats internalize this basic set of messages that you’re delivering here, which is that people just don’t think that they need to fear Democrats. They don’t need to fear Democratic accountability, might be the way to put it.

They need to fear Trump’s corrupt pressure more. And we talk constantly about the need for a rebalancing, and that’s an area where we really need a rebalancing. Corporations need to see the Democratic Congress as a formidable force for accountability in a way that I think maybe they just do not right now. Don’t you think?

Gurri: Yes, I agree. And that’s why I think some pressure should be put on state governments as well, because they have executive branches that can do things akin to what Trump could do. When California let the merger go through with Skydance and WB Discovery, that was terrible. They should not have done that.

That was, like, a clear case where they had the power to make an impact, and they did not. So we need to be applying pressure to state Democrats. We need to be applying pressure to congressional Democrats to do their jobs.

Sargent: Just to go back to a point you raised earlier, this election was a major cultural statement, of the sort that people kept mistakenly reading into the 2024 election. This was a huge outpouring of energy in the direction of accountability, and really a very strong repudiation of corporate elite impunity, it seems to me, with the data centers factoring so heavily, and Elon Musk being portrayed kind of as the guy who wants to buy a senator in Texas, and so forth. I mean, if we’re going to talk about cultural shifts in the country, there’s a big one, right? Isn’t there?

Gurri: Right. No, and I mean, just think about it. The Democrats have just expanded their coalition. The Democrats were already a very complicated coalition before this election, and they’ve just radically expanded it to include, like, a seat in Mississippi, you know, and Texas, right?

So it’s just gotten broader than it has been in decades. And so an issue like trans rights and immigration, and even, like, foreign policy with Israel and things like that—these are issues that there are genuine divides in the party about. But accountability for the crimes of the Trump administration is not something that codes left or right, or pro-Israel or anti-Israel.

That is something that can very easily unify this very broad coalition, which could be very powerful if they’re willing to go the distance. So hopefully they will, because they have every reason to. Voters have sent a very clear signal.

Sargent: Yes. And in fact, Democrats in all corners of the country, in every different type of district and state, won with a message about elite impunity and the need to put an end to that with the force of the federal government, with the force of the U.S. Congress. And so it would be unthinkable for them to punt on this.

I don’t think they will. Where do you see it going? I do think that most Democrats really understand that this was the nature of their victory, and I do think that they will act on that in some sense. There’s going to be a lot of headwinds that they’ll face that are structural and so forth.

But as long as they really push on every front and use every lever that’s at their disposal, I think that things could move in a positive direction. What’s your overall prognosis?

Gurri: So right now, the committee chairs in Congress, the ones that will be the heads of them next year, are very fiery in the rhetoric about what they intend to do. And most important of all, the one who will be the chair of the Oversight Committee in the House, Robert Garcia, a representative from California, has been very vocal about wanting to go after everything that has been going on.

I think it’s going to be hard, and it’s going to be a multiyear effort, because this is not something that is going to be fixed even if somehow—which they won’t be able to—but even if somehow they were able to send Jensen Huang to jail or something.

It’s not going to fix what is a general culture-of-impunity problem among tech CEOs and billionaires specifically, but sort of this class in general. It’s going to take real work. It’s going to take more than one congressional term—you know, session—to do it. So I would say it can be done. It will at least partly be done, probably, by this Congress.

But it’s going to be a long project that’s going to take a lot of pain, because these people do stand to control a lot of the economic power in the country, and hurting them does actually mean accepting stock markets going down sometimes as a result, which is very politically difficult to do.

Sargent: It is. And I think that if Democrats handle this correctly, which I expect that they mostly will, they’ll be able to frame the stakes for the 2028 election in really a useful way.

I’m very optimistic that 2028 could look very good coming out of these two years. Folks, if you want to follow more of Adam Gurri, check out LiberalCurrents.com. I’m a regular reader. It does outstanding work. Adam, thanks so much for coming on, man.

Gurri: Thanks for having me on.

items.title: Trump’s Vile Nvidia Spin Wrecked by Leaks From His Own Intel Officials
items.content_text: In an interview with CNBC, Donald Trump openly flaunted his role in pressuring Nvidia’s board to rehire its leader, Jensen Huang, despite Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Trump also declared that U.S. officials informed Nvidia that Huang doesn’t pose a national security threat. Yet this comes even as the The New York Times just reported on leaked intelligence showing the woman who had the affair with Huang was in touch with a senior Chinese spy figure during that period. Per the Times, this is a key reason U.S. intelligence was so concerned about the situation. These revelations badly undercut Trump’s pro-Huang spin. They also suggest intel sources want Trump’s pressure for his reinstatement to appear more dubious. We talked to Adam Gurri, the publisher of Liberal Currents, who’s been writing well about these developments. We discuss how Trump’s personalist dictator inclinations are shaping this scandal, why Nvidia doing Trump’s bidding is a bad omen, and why the incoming Democratic Congress must make breaking elite impunity a central mission. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: The Democrats Never Needed a Liberal Joe Rogan
items.content_text:
In the run-up to the 2024 election, there was seemingly endless discussion about the growing political influence of podcasts and other new media. Kamala Harris appeared on shows such as Alex Cooper’s Call Her Daddy, while Donald Trump spoke to Theo Von and others. Whether or not Harris would appear on Joe Rogan’s podcast was a topic worthy of national attention. After Harris lost, there was a broad public debate about which staffers were to blame for her not appearing on Rogan’s show, as if that appearance would have affected the results. (Subsequent reporting suggested that Rogan actually didn’t want to interview Harris and created numerous barriers to do so.)

Harris’s loss begot months of panic in Democratic circles about the party’s alleged disadvantage in new media. According to the conventional wisdom, Democrats needed their own Joe Rogan, a cadre of liberal influencers and podcasters, and mastery of the “attention” economy, which was supposedly the key to modern political success. California Governor Gavin Newsom started a podcast explicitly targeted at moderate and conservative men, with Steve Bannon and Charlie Kirk among his first guests. The victory of Zohran Mamdani, whose clever videos on social media helped his rise, supposedly validated this idea that Democrats mastering new media was crucial to winning.

Or maybe not. Democrats this month won by the largest margin for either party in an election in decades. They did that in a media environment that is fairly similar to 2024. There isn’t a liberal Joe Rogan, and the party didn’t spend much time courting the real-life conservative-leaning one, either. Nor did Democrats spend much time on Cooper’s show. Many Democratic candidates spoke to podcasters and influencers and were creative in their uses of social media, but the party was also heavily reliant on ads and traditional media. Old-school candidates such as North Carolina’s Roy Cooper easily won their races, as did younger figures such as Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico.

So what happened? It’s hard to say for sure, but let me offer a few theses.

The simplest and most obvious explanation is that Donald Trump governed in such an unpopular, ineffective way that it turned off voters who consumed traditional media, new media, both, and neither. Everyone in America heard about the invasion of Minneapolis by the Trump administration and the killings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti. Everyone saw gas prices surge after the war in Iran. Voters didn’t need a podcast to explain what was happening in their own lives.

The analyses of Democratic media strategies assumed an electoral environment that was close to 50–50, as most national campaigns have been since 2000. But a party’s podcast and social media strategy may not matter much if its base is highly motivated, the other party’s is depressed, and swing voters hate the incumbent president.

But I don’t think American voters turned on Trump based on events alone. Americans learn facts and narratives about politicians and government through the media. And the media environment was dramatically different in 2025–2026 than in 2024 in one way: The mainstream media focused mostly on the foibles of Republicans, instead of Democrats.

As I argued when Joe Biden was president, the mainstream media consistently delivers a torrent of negative news about whomever is in the Oval Office. That coverage approach comes from a good place. “Comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable” is a mantra in journalism. Outlets such as The New York Times and ProPublica pride themselves on their in-depth investigations that find malfeasance, particularly in the executive branch. After all, perhaps no person in the world is more powerful and comfortable than the American president.

But the effects of that approach are that the mistakes of every presidential administration get extensive coverage, their successes less so, and they end up declining in popularity. With the exception of the start and tail end of Barack Obama’s presidency, U.S. commanders in chief have been continually unpopular for the last 20 years. Trump deserved that negative coverage in ways that Biden and Obama didn’t. That said, it was entirely predictable that Democrats would benefit from the media’s anti-incumbent bias once Trump was in office. You don’t need new media as much if the old media is busy highlighting the president’s mistakes.

A third theory is that perhaps all of that social media and new media did matter. That Democrats won everywhere makes me skeptical that media strategies mattered that much. But the Democratic Party went from being led by Biden and his very old-guard staff to letting a thousand media flowers bloom. There was a ton more podcasting and social media use in 2026. Perhaps all the MeidasTouch hits and viral videos actually did give Democrats an advantage in the attention economy that increased their margin of victory nationally and in key swing states.

I’m more convinced by the first two theories (everyone hated Trump so the media didn’t matter and the mainstream media hurt the incumbent president) than the third. But there is one effect of the Democratic media innovations that is more clear: Leftists and progressives developed strategies and networks that helped them in primaries. It is hard to see Mamdani winning the mayoral primary in New York without his social media presence, because he was so far down in the polls at first that he wasn’t getting much mainstream coverage. Progressive candidates, particularly El-Sayed, were boosted by Drop Site News, Zeteo, Hasan Piker, and other leftist outlets and personalities.

I’m not sure how much that network mattered in the general election. But with the 2028 Democratic primary starting soon, those leftist outlets will again play a role.

New media’s potential role in primaries isn’t the only reason for Democrats to keep investing and innovating in alternatives to the mainstream. There will likely again be a Democratic president—hopefully in 2029. The mainstream media will likely amplify that president’s miscues, as it did with Obama and Biden, and largely drop coverage of the authoritarian right. One of the big questions of this era is whether a pro-democracy party can maintain popularity and consistently win elections, or if we are doomed to toggle between democracy and authoritarianism. A media ecosystem that doesn’t downplay incumbent party governing failures but also highlights successes would be particularly valuable to a future Democratic president.

Gavin Newsom didn’t need to start a podcast or host terrible conservatives. Alex Cooper’s audience couldn’t lift Harris to victory, and Joe Rogan’s wouldn’t have, either. And in a world where Abigail Spanberger and Roy Cooper easily won elections, the most effective politicians aren’t necessarily the best ones at getting attention. But the best analysis is that while new media matters, the old media matters even more—and neither is that important if the president is so cruel and inept that it’s obvious to everyone.

items.title: Why the Supreme Court’s Hypocritical Stance on Prisoners Matters
items.content_text:
The Supreme Court heard oral arguments earlier this month in Nielsen v. Watanabe, where it will decide whether a Hawaii man who allegedly experienced medical mistreatment in prison can personally sue those responsible for damages. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals concluded last year that he could because there was an implied cause of action in the Eighth Amendment that allowed it.

It appears unlikely that the justices will agree. The Supreme Court has disfavored these type of claims for the last thirty years, and the six-justice conservative majority sounded unwilling to extend them further. Such actions should be created by Congress, they have argued, not through judge-made law. The net result will be an even more difficult legal environment for prisoners whose constitutional rights are violated.

What stands out about the case—and, indeed, about the court’s overall approach to what are known as “Bivens claims”—is how the court approaches this debate between legislative and judicial power in other, similar circumstances. In the near future, the court’s decision will likely tell Americans that it is Congress’s responsibility to decide when and how people can sue government officials to defend their constitutional rights. The nation’s experience with qualified immunity tells a different story.

This particular case arose when the plaintiff, Kekai Watanabe, was assaulted by other prisoners at a federal prison in Honolulu in 2021. During the attack, they repeatedly bludgeoned him with a weighted sock. Watanabe asked to see prison medical staff later that night and complained to guards about “severe pain and headaches,” according to court filings. He saw Francis Nielsen, a member of the prison’s nursing staff, a few days later, at which point he noted that he was suffering from agonizing back pain, as well.

“When Watanabe requested treatment at a hospital, Nielsen refused, telling him, ‘you are not going to’ the hospital and to ‘stop being a cry baby,’” his lawyers told the justices in their brief. He then spent the following two months in solitary confinement. “Watanabe was not taken to a hospital or examined by a specialist; he received only intermittent and short-term treatment for pain, often over-the-counter medication,” they explained.

Seven months later, Watanabe finally received an x-ray that revealed the extent of his injuries: a fractured coccyx, from which bone chips had migrated into other parts of his lower torso. “Although prison officials agreed to allow Watanabe to receive treatment from a specialist, that never happened,” his lawyers told the justice. He was ultimately released from custody in 2024, three years after the original attack, but “remains in tremendous pain today.”

While he was still incarcerated in 2022, Watanabe sued Nielsen and other prison officials for damages in their personal capacity for violating his Eighth Amendment rights with substandard medical care. There is no federal law that allows Watanabe to bring this kind of claim against a federal official. But courts have recognized other implied causes of action in the Fourth and Eighth Amendment contexts. These claims are known as Bivens claims after the 1971 case Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Agents, which established them.

In Bivens, the Supreme Court held that a wronged plaintiff could sue federal agents for damages in their personal capacity for violating their Fourth Amendment rights against unlawful searches and seizures. No act of Congress authorized these claims, but a 6–3 majority reasoned that it could be inferred from broader common-law principles. “Of course, the Fourth Amendment does not in so many words provide for its enforcement by an award of money damages for the consequences of its violation,” Justice William Brennan wrote for the court. “But it is … well settled that, where legal rights have been invaded, and a federal statute provides for a general right to sue for such invasion, federal courts may use any available remedy to make good the wrong done.”

“[The agents] seek to treat the relationship between a citizen and a federal agent unconstitutionally exercising his authority as no different from the relationship between two private citizens,” Brennan wrote. “In so doing, they ignore the fact that power, once granted, does not disappear like a magic gift when it is wrongfully used. An agent acting—albeit unconstitutionally—in the name of the United States possesses a far greater capacity for harm than an individual trespasser exercising no authority other than his own.”

Bivens was decided in the twilight years of the Supreme Court’s liberal majority, and more moderate and conservative justices who followed often declined to extend it. Only twice since then has the court allowed similar implied causes of action to go forward: for sex discrimination by federal officials in the 1979 case Davis v. Pressman and for Eighth Amendment violations in the 1980 case Carlson v. Green. The latter case also involved medical mistreatment: The plaintiff’s son suffered an asthma attack in prison, received no medical treatment for eight hours, then received highly negligent medical treatment that contributed to his death.

In Nielsen, the prison officials hope to persuade the justices to do one of two things. One solution for them would be to overturn Bivens and Carlson altogether. “The Court has repudiated its reasoning; it is unworkable; and no reliance favors retention,” they claimed in their brief for the court. “Leaving Bivens on the books gives plaintiffs false hope, burdens defendants, and deters Congress from exercising its rightful role.” Alternatively, they said, the court could decline to extend Carlson to this specific context.

It seems unlikely that the court will choose the first option. Justice Brett Kavanaugh pointed out to Lucas Walker, who argued for the officials, that Congress “has had 55 years since Bivens and 46 years since Carlson” to override those rulings itself and hadn’t done it. “It seems like Congress, in fact, has left Bivens and Carlson where they stood,” he added, “and Congress has operated against that backdrop.” He noted that this wasn’t simply a matter of pure congressional inaction: Lawmakers had superseded the sex-discrimination claim in Davis with legislation, perhaps in part because the original defendant of the lawsuit was a former member of Congress.

Chief Justice John Roberts also pointed out that the Justice Department, which the court allowed to participate in the case, had specifically not asked the justices to overturn Bivens or Carlson. “I wonder if you have any insight into why or at least why shouldn’t we, on that question, defer to their expertise and experience?” he asked Walker, who said that limiting Carlson but not overturning Bivens might confuse the lower courts. “I mean, on the other hand, it could be viewed as a cautious, incremental approach to such a fundamental question,” Roberts responded.

The court’s second option, to narrow Carlson, seems more likely to be the outcome. There is one major difference between Carlson and Watanabe: The former died as a result of the prison staff’s malpractice, while the latter survived to sue for damages. (Carlson’s mother brought that case on behalf of his estate.) The court’s “death is different” mindset is a familiar one in Eighth Amendment cases. Though it diminishes Watanabe’s suffering, there is also a functional difference in outcomes. Carlson could not have turned to administrative proceedings for relief, nor obtained an injunction against the medical staff for the future. He was already dead. It was, as the court has said elsewhere in the Bivens context, “damages or nothing.”

Multiple justices asked questions along these lines, including Justice Elena Kagan, who may have been trying to steer her colleagues to a less extreme outcome. It fell to Justice Sonia Sotomayor to note that Carlson’s holding had other purposes, as well—namely, to serve as a deterrent for future prison officials against similar levels of medical negligence. Ideally, those officials would respect each prisoner’s constitutional rights at all times. But sometimes the fear of being sued (and especially the fear of losing a lawsuit and a lot of money with it) can be a powerful motivator for virtuous conduct. “There’s nothing in the alternatives you’re suggesting that’s going to address that deterrence aspect, correct?” Sotomayor asked Walker. He replied that whether a cause of action provides “proper deterrence” is “something that Congress, rather than federal courts, needs to calibrate.”

The Supreme Court itself has said the same thing, as Justice Clarence Thomas noted in the 2022 case Egbert v. Boule. The justices declined in that case to find an implied cause of action for a Fourth Amendment excessive force claim. Though they did not overturn Bivens et al., Thomas quoted other recent decisions to emphasize that recognizing implied causes of action for violating constitutional rights was now a “disfavored judicial activity.” The Constitution’s separation of powers was central to his argument.

We have come “to appreciate more fully the tension between” judicially created causes of action and “the Constitution’s separation of legislative and judicial power.” At bottom, creating a cause of action is a legislative endeavor. Courts engaged in that unenviable task must evaluate a “range of policy considerations … at least as broad as the range … a legislature would consider.” Those factors include “economic and governmental concerns,” “administrative costs,” and the “impact on governmental operations systemwide.” Unsurprisingly, Congress is “far more competent than the Judiciary” to weigh such policy considerations. And the Judiciary’s authority to do so at all is, at best, uncertain.

This deep reverence for Congress and its powers would be laudable if it weren’t unconvincing. Imagine, if you will, that everything about this case was the same except for one thing: Watanabe was being held in a state prison instead of a federal one, and the officials were state employees instead of federal ones. In this hypothetical, Watanabe would not need to rely on an implied cause of action to sue them for violating his constitutional rights in federal court. He could invoke Section 1983 instead. The Reconstruction-era provision of federal law allows plaintiffs to sue state and local officials for damages in federal court for violating their federal constitutional rights.

While Bivens claims are rare nowadays, Section 1983 is a well-established mechanism for bringing lawsuits against state and local officials. In this scenario, the hypothetical Watanabe could have filed a Section 1983 lawsuit against the hypothetical state prison officials for violating his Eighth Amendment rights. This is the implied solution when the Supreme Court says that it is Congress’s responsibility to act on this matter, not theirs. It would also reflect the court’s stated preference for statutory causes of action over judge-made ones.

Except when the high court reviews those kinds of cases, the shoe is suddenly on the other foot. The Supreme Court has imposed multiple limits on Section 1983 claims by allowing state officials to invoke qualified immunity when they are sued in federal court. Qualified immunity is not a product of Congress’s measured consideration of how to deter abuses by state officials while also giving them enough leeway to do their jobs. It is not even part of Section 1983 at all. It is a judicially created defense for state officials that often defeats otherwise legitimate claims. (The Supreme Court also allows federal officials to invoke it, but since Bivens claims are rare, nearly all cases that the justices hear on it are state ones.)

To overcome qualified immunity, a Section 1983 plaintiff must not only allege that a violation of their federal constitutional rights happened but that the violation ran counter to “clearly established law” at the time. The high court’s stated intent was to ensure that only “plainly incompetent” officials or those who “knowingly violate” the law can be sued.
